_comment: Daily Bread — the portions served on the home page, one per calendar day. Every portion is hand-chosen and its reflection is written for that passage alone: who is speaking, to whom, and what the verses themselves say. There is no stock wording shared between portions. Each is a passage of two or more consecutive verses that begins where a sentence begins and ends where one lands. Verse text is NOT stored here: it is read at run time from assets/text/<book>.json so the wording always matches the canon. After editing, run python3 scripts/build_daily_bread.py — it checks every entry and regenerates assets/DailyBread.js.

pool.reflection: Before there is anything to see, three things are already there: Aluahim, His Ruach moving on the face of the waters, and His word. Formless, empty and dark is where He begins, not where He gives up. He said “Let light come to be,” and it came to be.

pool.theme: Seedtime and harvest shall not cease
pool.reflection: Noaḥ has just stepped out onto a washed earth, and Yahuah says this in His heart: though man's inclination is evil from his youth, never again. Every sunrise, every harvest and every turning of winter into summer since has been that promise being kept.

Aḇram is told what to leave, land, relatives and his father's house, but not where he is going: only “a land which I show you.” The berakah is promised to the one who goes. And it was never meant to stop with him: “in you all the clans of the earth shall be baruk.”

A childless old man is brought outside and told to count what cannot be counted. Nothing in his tent had changed when he came back in. He “believed in Yahuah,” and that believing, not any deed, is what was reckoned to him for righteousness.

Ya'aqoḇ is a runaway sleeping on a stone when the promise finds him: “I am with you and shall guard you wherever you go.” He wakes and says what many have said looking back on a hard night: “Truly, Yahuah is in this place and I did not know it.”

Yoseph does not pretend the pit and the selling were anything but evil: “you intended evil against me.” He simply sets a second intention over the first. The brothers meant harm, Aluahim meant the keeping alive of many people, and the man who believes that can afford to speak kindly.

Mosheh asks the question every messenger must be able to answer: whose word is this? The reply is not a title but a Name, Yahuah, Aluahim of Aḇraham, Yahtsḥaq and Ya'aqoḇ: “This is My Name forever and this is My Remembrance to all generations.” It was given to be remembered and spoken.

The sea is in front of them and Pharaoh's chariots are behind. Mosheh gives the people nothing to do except not be afraid: “stand still and see the deliverance of Yahuah, which He does for you today.” The fighting is His. Their part is to keep still, and then to walk when the way opens.

pool.theme: Yah is my strength and song
pool.reflection: This is the first song in Scripture, sung on the far shore with the sea closed behind them. Notice what Yasharal sings about: not their own escape but Him, “He is highly exalted.” The deliverance they walked through that night became the song they carried afterwards.

Before a single command is given at Sinai, Yahuah reminds them what He has already done: “I bore you on eagles' wings and brought you to Myself.” The carrying came first and the berith second. Obedience here is the answer of a people already rescued.

Mosheh has a nation to lead through a wilderness, and he does not ask for a map. He asks, “show me Your way and let me know You.” The answer is better than directions: “My Presence does go and I shall give you rest.”

Mosheh asked to see His esteem, and what he was given was the Name with its meaning: compassionate, showing chen, patient, great in kindness and truth. Kindness is kept for thousands; crookedness is answered to the third and fourth generation. Both are true of Him, and the kindness runs far longer.

The command Yahusha called the second greatest stands here in the Torah, among very plain instructions: do not hate in your heart, speak to your neighbour rather than resent him, take no vengeance, bear no grudge. The reason given is three words long: “I am Yahuah.”

Yahuah promises more than rescue; He promises to walk in the midst of His people and be their Aluahim. Then He names what He has already done: “I have broken the bars of your yoke and made you walk upright.” A people freed by Him are not meant to go about bent over.

pool.theme: Yahuah bless you and guard you
pool.reflection: These are the words Yahuah Himself gave Aharon and his sons to speak over Yasharal, and His Name is in every line. He blesses and guards, He makes His face shine and shows chen, He lifts up His face and gives shalom. The kohanim only say it; He is the one who does it.

pool.theme: He has baruk, and I do not reverse it
pool.reflection: Bil‛am was hired to curse Yasharal and found he could only bless. What he says about Yahuah is the reason: “Al is not a man, to lie.” Has He said, and would He not do it? No hired voice can reverse what He has spoken over His people.

Mosheh is speaking of a day when Yasharal would be scattered for their own unfaithfulness, and even then: “from there you shall seek Yahuah your Aluahim and shall find.” No place of distress is too far to seek from, because He is “a compassionate Al” who does not forget the berith.

The Shema: Yahuah our Aluahim, Yahuah is one. Because He is one, the love asked for is undivided too, all your heart, all your being, all your might. When Yahusha was asked which command is first of all, this is the one He recited.

Why did Yahuah choose Yasharal? Not for their numbers; they were “the least of all peoples.” The only reason given is the reason itself: because He loved them and was guarding the oath He swore. A love that never rested on their size cannot be lost when they are small.

Mosheh explains the forty years: the hunger and the manna were both lessons, given “to make you know that man does not live by bread alone but by every Word that comes from the mouth of Yahuah.” Yahusha answered the tempter in the wilderness with this very line.

pool.theme: What is Yahuah asking of you
pool.reflection: After the golden calf and the second set of tablets, Mosheh gathers everything into one question. To fear Him, walk in His ways, love Him, serve Him with all your heart, guard His commands. And he adds the words that change how the whole list is heard: “for your good.”

pool.theme: The Word is very near you
pool.reflection: No one has to climb into the shamayim or cross the sea to find out what Yahuah wants. Mosheh says the command is “not too hard for you, nor is it far off.” It is in your mouth and in your heart, and the last three words tell you what it is there for: “to do it.”

Mosheh sets it out before the whole nation with the shamayim and the earth as witnesses: life and death, the berakah and the curse. Then he says what choosing life actually is: to love Yahuah, obey His voice and cling to Him, “for He is your life and the length of your days.”

Mosheh is a hundred and twenty and will not cross the Yarden. What he hands to the people, and then to Yahusha son of Nun before their eyes, is not a strategy but a fact said twice: Yahuah goes before you, “He does not fail you nor forsake you.” The command not to fear rests on that.

pool.theme: The Rock, His work is perfect
pool.reflection: This is how the song of Mosheh opens, the song he taught Yasharal just before his death. After forty years of wilderness, complaints and burials, his verdict on Yahuah is this: perfect work, right-ruling ways, “an Al of truth and without unrighteousness.”

These are among the last words of Mosheh's last berakah. He looks up and sees Al “riding the shamayim to help you”; he looks down and sees the arms. The Aluahim of old is a refuge above you and a support beneath you, and there is no falling lower than His arms.

pool.theme: Do not let this Book depart from your mouth
pool.reflection: Yahusha son of Nun is taking over from Mosheh, and the charge he receives ties courage to the Torah: speak it, meditate on it day and night, do it. Then the command, “Be strong and courageous,” with its reason: “Yahuah your Aluahim is with you wherever you go.”

pool.theme: I and my house, we serve Yahuah
pool.reflection: At the end of his life Yahusha does not let Yasharal drift. There are the mighty ones their fathers served beyond the River, the ones of Mitsrayim, the ones of the land, and there is Yahuah. “Choose for yourselves this day.” He has already chosen, and he speaks for his whole house.

pool.theme: There is no rock like our Aluahim
pool.reflection: Ḥannah had wept and prayed for years without a child. This is her prayer on the day she brings Shamu'Al to the House of Yahuah, and she hardly mentions the boy. Her heart rejoices “in Yahuah.” The gift has turned her eyes to the Giver: no one is qadash like Him.

Shamu'Al is sure that Yahshai's tall eldest son must be the anointed one. He is wrong, and Yahuah tells him why: man looks at what the eyes can see, “but Yahuah looks at the heart.” The one He chose that day was the youngest, out with the sheep, whom no one had thought to call in.

pool.theme: You are my lamp, O Yahuah
pool.reflection: Dawiḏ sang this on the day Yahuah delivered him from all his enemies and from Sha’ul. Looking back over the caves and the running, he does not claim he saw clearly; he says Yahuah made his darkness light. “His way is perfect,” and He is a shield to all who take refuge in Him.

Shelomoh stands before the finished House and blesses the qahal with a statement of record: “There has not failed one Word of all His good word.” Then he asks for what a faithful Aluahim still has to give, that He would incline their hearts to Himself so they walk in His ways.

Aliyahu has run for his life to the mountain of Aluahim. A ruach tears the rocks, the earth quakes, fire passes, and Yahuah is in none of them. Then comes a still small voice, and it asks a worn-out naḇi a question: “What are you doing here?” He had come close enough to hear it.

pool.theme: Open his eyes and let him see
pool.reflection: The servant counts horses and chariots around the city and asks what they are to do. Alisha's answer is a matter of arithmetic: “those who are with us are more than those who are with them.” He does not pray for more help to come. He prays that the young man will see the help already there.

pool.theme: A Child shall be born unto us
pool.reflection: Yashayahu speaks to a people walking in darkness and gives them a Son, with the rule on His shoulder and a Name: Wonder, Counsellor, Strong Al, Father of Continuity, Prince of Shalom. His rule and His shalom have no end. “The ardour of Yahuah of hosts does this.”

pool.theme: A Rod from the stump of Yahshai
pool.reflection: The house of Dawiḏ would be cut down to a stump, and from the stump a Sprout comes. The Ruach of Yahuah rests on Him: wisdom and understanding, counsel and might, knowledge and the fear of Yahuah. He does not judge by what His eyes see or His ears hear.

“See, Al is my deliverance.” Then a line from the song at the sea: Yah is my strength and my song. Deliverance is pictured as a fountain, and the people come to draw from it with joy. At the Festival of Booths water was drawn and poured out with this verse.

pool.theme: He shall swallow up death forever
pool.reflection: On His mountain Yahuah makes a feast, and there He swallows up death and wipes the tears from every face. Then the people speak: “See, this is our Aluahim. We have waited for Him and He saves us.” The waiting comes to an end.

This is from a song to be sung in the land of Yahuḏah. The one whose mind is steadfast is guarded “in perfect shalom,” and the reason is that he trusts. So the song turns to everyone: trust in Yahuah forever, for in Yah there is “a rock of ages.”

pool.theme: This is the Way, walk in it
pool.reflection: Yashayahu speaks to people who had looked to Mitsrayim for help. He promises a day when Yahuah answers at the sound of their cry and their Teacher is no longer hidden. Whenever they drift right or left, a word comes from behind: “This is the Way, walk in it.”

pool.theme: Say to those with anxious heart
pool.reflection: This is something to do for someone else: strengthen weak hands, steady weak knees, and say to the anxious, “Be strong, do not fear!” The courage does not come from the speaker. It comes from the news he carries: “your Aluahim comes … He is coming to save you.”

pool.theme: The Word of our Aluahim stands forever
pool.reflection: A voice says “Cry out,” and the message begins with our frailty. All flesh is grass and its loveliness like the flower of the field, here and then withered. One thing stands: “the Word of our Aluahim stands forever.” Kĕpha says this is the Word announced to us as Besorah.

pool.theme: He gathers the lambs with His arm
pool.reflection: Two pictures of one arm. The Master Yahuah comes with a strong hand, “and His arm rules for Him.” The same arm gathers the lambs and carries them against His chest, and He gently leads those with young. His strength is used to carry the weak.

pool.theme: Lift up your eyes on high
pool.reflection: Yahuah asks to whom He can be compared, and tells His tired people to look up at the stars. He brings out their host by number and calls each by name, and “not one is missing.” He who does not lose track of a single star has not lost track of them.

Yasharal had been saying, “My way is hidden from Yahuah.” The naḇi answers: have you not heard? The Creator of the ends of the earth does not faint or grow weary. Even youths give out. Those who wait on Him exchange their strength for His, and rise, run, and walk.

pool.theme: I am holding your right hand
pool.reflection: Yahuah speaks to Yasharal His servant. “Do not fear” is said twice, with a reason each time: “I am with you,” and “I, Yahuah your Aluahim, am holding your right hand.” The right hand of His righteousness holds theirs. Those who strive against them come to nothing.

pool.theme: I have called you by your name
pool.reflection: He who created Ya'aqoḇ and formed Yasharal says three things: I have redeemed you, I have called you by name, you are Mine. Then comes “when,” and not “if”: when you pass through the waters and walk through the fire. He does not promise a way around them. “I am with you.”

pool.theme: I am doing what is new
pool.reflection: Yahuah has just recalled the way He made through the sea, and then says not to dwell on it. He is not only the Aluahim of what He did once. “See, I am doing what is new”: a way in the wilderness this time, and rivers in the desert.

pool.theme: Return to Me, for I shall redeem you
pool.reflection: “I have formed you, you are My servant … do not forget Me.” Then Yahuah says what He does with their transgressions: He wipes them out like a cloud, like morning mist that is gone when the sun is up. The call to return follows the wiping out.

pool.theme: Even to grey hairs I carry
pool.reflection: The chapter opens with the idols of Baḇal loaded onto weary animals, mighty ones that have to be carried. Yahuah says the opposite of Himself. He has carried Yasharal from the womb and will carry them to old age: “I have made and I bear and I carry and rescue.”

pool.theme: Inscribed on the palms of My hands
pool.reflection: Tsiyon says, “Yahuah has forsaken me and Yahuah has forgotten me.” He answers with the strongest human bond there is, a mother and her nursing child, and says even that may fail: “I'll never forget you.” She is inscribed on the palms of His hands.

pool.theme: I, I am He who comforts you
pool.reflection: The ransomed of Yahuah come back to Tsiyon singing, and sorrow and sighing flee away. Then He speaks: “I, I am He who comforts you.” With such a Comforter, He asks why they should be afraid of a man who dies and withers like grass.

A runner comes over the mountains toward a ruined city, and his feet are called pleasant because of what he brings: shalom, good news, deliverance, and the word “Your Aluahim reigns!” The watchmen see it first and shout. Then the waste places themselves are told to sing.

pool.theme: By His stripes we are healed
pool.reflection: Yashayahu speaks of the Servant of Yahuah, and every line trades places. The sicknesses and pains are ours and He carried them. The transgressions are ours and He was pierced. We went astray like sheep, each to his own way, “and Yahuah has laid on Him the crookedness of us all.”

pool.theme: My kindness is not removed from you
pool.reflection: Yahuah speaks to Tsiyon as to a wife taken back. The wrath was “for a moment”; the kindness is everlasting. He swears it as He swore to Noaḥ about the flood. Mountains may be removed and hills shaken, but not His kindness and not His berith of shalom.

The invitation goes to the thirsty and to those with no silver, and it tells them to buy: wine and milk “without silver and without price.” Then a question for everyone spending themselves on what does not satisfy. “Incline your ear and come to Me. Hear, so that your being lives.”

There is a time to seek: “while He is to be found … while He is near.” The wrong man is told to leave his way and the unrighteous his thoughts, and to return. What he will find when he does is told in advance: compassion, and an Aluahim who “pardons much.”

pool.theme: As the shamayim are higher than the earth
pool.reflection: These lines come straight after the promise that He pardons much, and they explain it. Men would not forgive like that. “My thoughts are not your thoughts.” The distance between the shamayim and the earth is how far His ways of compassion are above ours.

pool.theme: My Word does not return to Me empty
pool.reflection: Rain and snow do not go back up until they have watered the earth and given seed to the sower and bread to the eater. His Word is like that: it accomplishes what He sent it for. For the exiles that meant going out with joy and being led in shalom.

pool.theme: The fast that I have chosen
pool.reflection: The people fasted and asked why Yahuah took no notice. He tells them the fast He chooses: loosen the cords of wrongness, free the oppressed, share your bread with the hungry, bring the poor into your house, clothe the naked. “Then your light would break forth like the morning.”

When you call, He answers, “Here I am.” The promise is for the one who takes away the yoke and the pointing finger, and extends his own being to the hungry. His darkness becomes like noon. Yahuah guides him continually and satisfies him in drought, and he becomes “like a watered garden,” a spring whose waters do not fail.

Tsiyon is told to get up and shine, and the reason is not anything in herself: “your light has come.” Darkness covers the earth and thick darkness the peoples, but Yahuah rises over her. Nations and sovereigns come toward that brightness.

pool.theme: The oil of joy for mourning
pool.reflection: Yahusha stood up in the congregation at Natsareth, read from this place, and said, “Today this Scripture has been filled in your hearing.” He was sent to the meek, the broken-hearted, the captives. He gives embellishment for ashes, the oil of joy for mourning, a garment of praise for heaviness.

The speaker is dressed by Another: garments of deliverance, a robe of righteousness, put on him as a bridegroom and a bride are adorned. So he rejoices greatly in Yahuah. And as a garden makes what is sown in it spring up, Yahuah will make righteousness and praise spring up before all nations.

Tsiyon had two names, Forsaken and Deserted. Yahuah gives her new ones: Ḥephtsiḇah, “My delight is in her,” and Married. She is a crown in His hand. The last line says how He feels about her: as the bridegroom rejoices over the bride, “so shall your Aluahim rejoice over you.”

pool.theme: We are the clay and You our potter
pool.reflection: This prayer comes from a people who have just confessed that their righteousnesses are as soiled rags. They do not argue their case. They say what they are to Him: “You are our Father … we are all the work of Your hand.” The appeal rests on belonging: “all of us are Your people.”

pool.theme: As one whom his mother comforts
pool.reflection: Yahuah extends shalom to Yahrushalayim like a river, and then describes His comfort in the tenderest picture He could use: a child carried on the hip and held on the knees. “As one whom his mother comforts, so I comfort you.”

pool.theme: Do not say, “I am a youth”
pool.reflection: Yirmayahu is told he was known before he was formed and set apart before he was born. His objection is his age and his speech. Yahuah does not argue about either. He says go where I send you, speak what I command you, and, “I am with you to deliver you.”

pool.theme: Let him who boasts boast of this
pool.reflection: Wisdom, might and riches are the three things people most often rest on, and all three are set aside. One thing is worth boasting in: to understand and know Yahuah, who does kindness, right-ruling and righteousness in the earth. “For in these I delight.”

pool.theme: A tree planted by the waters
pool.reflection: The verses just before describe the man who trusts in man: a shrub in the desert. This is the other man, whose trust is Yahuah. Heat comes and a year of drought comes, and he “does not see” it the same way, because his roots are spread out by the river.

Yirmayahu was shown two baskets of figs, and these words were spoken over the good ones, the exiles carried off to the land of the Chaldeans. Yahuah sets His eyes on them for good. The best of His promises to them is a gift inside: “a heart to know Me.”

This is from a letter Yirmayahu sent to the exiles in Baḇal, telling them to build houses and plant gardens because they would be there seventy years. In that long wait Yahuah says He knows His plans for them, “a future and an expectancy,” and that He will be found when they seek Him with all their heart.

These words are spoken to a people who had been torn down. “I have loved you with an everlasting love, therefore I shall draw you with kindness.” Then the promise: “I am going to build you again.” The maiden of Yasharal will take up her tambourines and dance once more.

Yahuah promises a berith unlike the one they broke. The Torah is the same, but it is written in a new place: “in their inward parts … on their hearts.” All shall know Him, from the least to the greatest, because He forgives their crookedness and remembers their sin no more.

Yirmayahu is shut up in the court of the guard and the city is under siege when this word comes. The One who made the earth and formed it gives a prisoner an open invitation: “Call unto Me and I shall answer you,” and show you great matters you have not known.

This is a promise to the exiles, whom those left in Yahrushalayim had written off as far from Yahuah. He will give them one heart and put a new ruach within them, taking away the heart of stone. The aim is the old berith promise: “they shall be My people and I shall be their Aluahim.”

pool.theme: I Myself shall search for My sheep
pool.reflection: The shepherds of Yasharal had fed themselves and let the flock scatter. So the Master Yahuah says, “I Myself.” He will search, seek out and deliver His sheep from every place they were scattered “in a day of cloud and thick darkness.” Yahusha called Himself the good shepherd.

pool.theme: I shall put My Ruach within you
pool.reflection: Yahuah lists what He will do, and every verb is His: sprinkle clean water, cleanse, give a new heart, take away the heart of stone, put His Ruach within. Then the walking in His laws follows: “I shall cause you to walk.” The obedience He requires He also gives.

pool.theme: He reveals deep and secret matters
pool.reflection: The sovereign had demanded his dream and its meaning on pain of death, and Dani'Al and his friends prayed through the night. This is his berakah when the answer came. Wisdom and might are His. He removes sovereigns and raises them up. “Light dwells with Him.”

Three young men stand before the furnace and the sovereign who built it. Their answer has two halves. “Our Al whom we serve is able to deliver us.” And, “But if not,” they still will not bow to the gold image. They would serve Him whether or not He rescued them.

These are the words of Dareyawesh, a gentile sovereign, in a decree sent to every people of his reign. He had spent a sleepless night over the lions' den and found Dani'Al alive in the morning. “He delivers and rescues.” A man who would not stop praying brought a sovereign to say so.

pool.theme: I shall take you as a bride forever
pool.reflection: Hoshea's own marriage was a picture of Yasharal's unfaithfulness, and this is what Yahuah says after it: He will take her as a bride again, and forever. He brings righteousness, right-ruling, kindness, compassion and trustworthiness. “And you shall know Yahuah.”

pool.theme: Let us pursue to know Yahuah
pool.reflection: “Come and let us turn back to Yahuah.” The One who tore is the One who heals; the One who struck binds up. On the third day He raises up. His going forth is as sure as the morning, and He comes “like the latter rain watering the earth.”

Yahuah remembers Yasharal's childhood as a father would: teaching the child to walk, holding him by the arms, healing him when he did not know who had done it. He drew them “with cords of love.” And then the most tender line: “I bent down, fed them.”

pool.theme: I shall be like the dew to Yasharal
pool.reflection: The last chapter of Hoshea gives the people words of return, and this is the answer they are promised. He will heal their backsliding and love them freely. Like dew He will come, and Yasharal will blossom like the lily, root like Leḇanon, and spread like an olive tree.

pool.theme: Tear your heart and not your garments
pool.reflection: A plague of locusts has stripped the land, and Yahuah says, “Yet even now.” He does not want torn clothes, the outward show of grief. He wants a heart that turns. The reason to turn is what He proclaimed of Himself to Mosheh: He shows chen and is compassionate, patient and of great kindness.

The fear is lifted in order, from the ground up: the soil, the beasts of the field, then the children of Tsiyon. Pastures spring up, the fig tree and the vine bear again, and the former and latter rain come down. The gladness has a source: “rejoice in Yahuah your Aluahim.”

pool.theme: The years the locust has eaten
pool.reflection: Yahuah does not promise only that the locusts will stop. He promises to repay the years they ate. His people will eat and be satisfied and praise His Name, and they will know He is in their midst. Twice He says it: “My people shall never be put to shame.”

pool.theme: I pour out My Ruach on all flesh
pool.reflection: Sons and daughters, old men and young men, male servants and female servants: no age, sex or station is passed over. Kĕpha stood up on the day of the Festival of Weeks and said, “This is what was spoken by the naḇi Yo'Al.”

The people of the northern reign said Yahuah was with them. Amos tells them how to make that true: seek good, hate evil, “set up right-ruling in the gate,” where the courts sat. Seeking Him cannot be separated from how the poor are treated at the gate.

Yonah prays from inside the fish, and his prayer is made of words from Tehillim that he had by heart. He had gone down as far as a man can go. “But You brought up my life from the pit.” He has not yet been put on dry land when he says, “Deliverance is of Yahuah.”

pool.theme: What does Yahuah require of you
pool.reflection: The worshipper keeps raising his offer: burnt offerings, thousands of rams, rivers of oil, even his first-born. He has missed the point, and Mikah says it was never hidden. “He has declared to you, O man, what is good”: do right, love kindness, and walk humbly with your Aluahim.

Mikah has looked around and found no upright man left in the land. “As for me, I look to Yahuah.” He does not deny that he has fallen or that he sits in the dark. He tells his enemy what is also true: “When I have fallen I have risen … Yahuah is a light to me.”

pool.theme: Who is an Al like You
pool.reflection: Mikah's own name means “Who is like Yah?”, and his book ends by answering it. No one else takes away crookedness and passes over transgression, because “He Himself delights in kindness.” He treads our crookednesses underfoot and throws all our sins into the depths of the sea.

pool.theme: If it lingers, wait for it
pool.reflection: Ḥaḇaqquq had asked how long, and climbed his watchtower to see what Yahuah would say. The answer was to write the vision plainly. It is for an appointed time and it will not lie. “If it lingers, wait for it.” Meanwhile the righteous one lives by his steadfastness.

Ḥaḇaqquq lists a farmer's whole livelihood and loses it line by line: fig, vine, olive, field, flock and herd. Then, “Yet.” His joy was resting on the Aluahim of his deliverance and not on the harvest. Yahuah is his strength and makes his feet like a deer's on the high places.

pool.theme: He rejoices over you with singing
pool.reflection: “Do not let your hands be weak,” Tsiyon is told, and the reason is who stands in her midst: Yahuah her Aluahim, mighty to save. Elsewhere His people sing over Him. Here He rejoices over them with joy, is silent in His love, and sings.

pool.theme: I shall gather those who were cast out
pool.reflection: These are the closing words of the book, and they are for the lame and the outcast. Yahuah will deal with those afflicting them, bring His people in, and turn their shame into praise in all the earth. It will happen, He says, “before your eyes.”

The returned exiles were building a House that looked like nothing beside the old one, and the old men wept to see it. Yahuah says “be strong” three times, to the governor, to the kohen gadol and to all the people. Then, “and work. For I am with you.” His Ruach remains in their midst.

pool.theme: I am coming to dwell in your midst
pool.reflection: The daughter of Tsiyon is told to sing because Yahuah is coming to live among her. Then the promise opens outward: “many gentiles shall be joined to Yahuah in that day and they shall become My people.” His dwelling among them was always meant to draw the nations in.

pool.theme: Not by might nor by power
pool.reflection: Zerubbaḇal faced a mountain of rubble and opposition with a small company of returned exiles. The word to him was that the House would not be finished by might or by power, “but by My Ruach.” The mountain becomes a plain, and the capstone is set with shouts of “Chen, chen to it!”

pool.theme: Speak the truth to one another
pool.reflection: Yahuah has just promised to do good to Yahrushalayim, and then says what His people are to do: speak the truth to one another, judge with truth and right-ruling in the gates, plot no evil against each other, love no false oath. These are things done between neighbours.

pool.theme: Your Sovereign is coming to you
pool.reflection: Tsiyon is told to shout, and then told what kind of Sovereign to look for: righteous, bringing deliverance, humble, riding on a donkey's colt. Yahusha rode into Yahrushalayim exactly so. He cuts off the chariot and the battle bow, and “He shall speak shalom to the nations.”

Some were saying it is worthless to serve Aluahim. Others, who feared Yahuah, spoke to one another, and He listened and heard. Their names were written before Him. “They shall be Mine,” He says, “on the day that I prepare a treasured possession.”

pool.theme: Like a tree planted by the rivers
pool.reflection: The first psalm sorts every life by where it is rooted. One man takes his direction from the counsel of the wrong, walking, then standing, then sitting. The other delights in the Torah of Yahuah and turns it over day and night, and he is the tree whose leaf does not wither.

By its ancient title, Dawiḏ sang this when he fled from his son Aḇshalom. A sovereign driven from his own city says Yahuah is his shield and “the One lifting up my head,” and then tells us the proof of it: he lay down, he slept, and he woke, “for Yahuah sustained me.”

pool.theme: More gladness than grain and wine
pool.reflection: Many are asking, “Who would show us good?” Dawiḏ asks for one thing, the light of Yahuah's face, and says it has put more gladness in his heart than other men have at harvest. That is why he can lie down in shalom: “You alone, O Yahuah, make me dwell in safety.”

pool.theme: In the morning You hear my voice
pool.reflection: Dawiḏ lays out his prayer in the morning and then does something easy to leave out: “I look up.” He prays as a man who expects to be answered. He calls Yahuah “my Sovereign and my Aluahim,” and brings Him the day before the day has brought anything.

The psalm has been full of bloodthirsty and deceitful men, and it closes on those who take refuge in Yahuah, who have cause to rejoice and shout for joy. The reason is the last line: “You surround him with chen as with a shield.” His favour stands on every side of the righteous.

pool.theme: What is man that You remember him?
pool.reflection: Dawiḏ looks at the night sky, the moon and the stars, and calls them the work of Yahuah's fingers. Against that he sets man, and the wonder is not that we are small. It is that He remembers and visits us, and has crowned the son of man with esteem and splendour.

Yahuah is “a refuge for the crushed one,” and the psalm says who trusts Him: those who know His Name. To know His Name is to know what He is like. And what He is like is this: “You have not forsaken those who seek You, O Yahuah.”

pool.theme: He has been good to me
pool.reflection: Four times this short psalm asks “How long?” Nothing in it says the answer came before the last verses. Dawiḏ simply turns: “But I have trusted in Your kindness.” He decides to sing while the question is still open, because of what Yahuah has already been to him.

pool.theme: At His right hand I am not shaken
pool.reflection: Dawiḏ has set Yahuah always before him, and his heart, his esteem and his flesh all rest on that. Kĕpha read these words aloud on the day of the Festival of Weeks as spoken of Mashiach, whose being was not left in the grave. The path of life leads into His presence, where joy is full.

pool.theme: My rock, my stronghold, my deliverer
pool.reflection: By its ancient title, Dawiḏ spoke this song on the day Yahuah delivered him from Sha’ul. He piles up names, rock, stronghold, deliverer, shield, horn, high tower, each one a place he had needed to hide. What had been true of the caves he says of Yahuah: “I take refuge in Him.”

There is a witness that never stops and never uses a word. Day pours out speech to day, night shows knowledge to night, and all of it says one thing: the esteem of Al and the work of His hand. Anyone who walks outside and looks up has been spoken to.

Dawiḏ has praised the Torah of Yahuah, and its light shows him himself: mistakes he cannot even discern, and presumptuous sins that want to rule him. So he asks to be kept, and offers what is closest to hand, his words and the meditation of his heart, to “my rock and my redeemer.”

This is a prayer said over the sovereign before battle. Other armies count chariots and horses, the best weapons of their day. Yasharal counts differently: “we remember the Name of Yahuah our Aluahim.” The saving might belongs to His right hand, not to anything they bring to the field.

Dawiḏ kept sheep before he kept a throne, and he knows what a shepherd does: leads to pasture and water, turns the sheep back, walks it through the dark valley with rod and staff. In the valley the psalm stops speaking about Him and speaks to Him: “You are with me.”

Four requests in two verses: show me, teach me, lead me, teach me. Dawiḏ does not ask for his own way to be made easier. He asks to be taught Yahuah's ways, and he is prepared to wait for the answer: “On You I wait all the day.”

pool.theme: He teaches sinners in the way
pool.reflection: Because Yahuah is good and straight, He does not leave sinners where they are; He teaches them the way. The ones who learn it are called “the meek,” those willing to be guided. To them every path of Yahuah turns out to be “kindness and truth.”

Dawiḏ names Yahuah three ways, my light, my deliverance, the refuge of my life, and asks the same question after each: whom should I fear? Evil-doers come, an army encamps, battle rises. He does not say they will not. He says, “Even then I would be trusting.”

Dawiḏ says what kept him going: he believed he would see the goodness of Yahuah “in the land of the living,” in this life and not only afterwards. Then he turns and speaks to us, and says it twice because once is not enough: “Wait, I say, on Yahuah!”

The order is worth following: his heart trusted, he was helped, and so his heart exults and he gives thanks with a song. Then Dawiḏ widens the prayer from himself to all the people: “be their Shepherd and bear them up forever.” What Yahuah has been to one, he asks for all.

The psalm has thundered with the voice of Yahuah over the waters, breaking cedars and shaking the wilderness. It ends with Him seated above the flood as Sovereign forever. And the One with that voice does this with it: He gives strength to His people and “blesses His people with shalom.”

Dawiḏ had been brought back from the edge of the grave, and he calls the kind ones of Yahuah to sing with him. His displeasure is for a moment; His delight is for life. Weeping may stay the night like a guest, but it is joy that comes in the morning.

pool.theme: My times are in Your hand
pool.reflection: Dawiḏ is surrounded, slandered and plotted against, and he says two short things. “You are my Aluahim.” “My times are in Your hand.” The hours he cannot control, and the day of his rescue, are held by Someone. Then he asks for the shining face spoken of in the berakah of the kohanim.

pool.theme: Be strong, all you who wait
pool.reflection: The psalm that began in distress ends by turning to everyone else: “Love Yahuah, all you His kind ones!” He guards the trustworthy. The strength Dawiḏ speaks of is not something worked up from inside: “let Him strengthen your heart,” he says, to all who are waiting for Yahuah.

Dawiḏ has just confessed his sin and found it covered, and now the One he hid from has become his hiding place. Then Yahuah Himself speaks: “Let Me instruct you and teach you in the way you should go.” He counsels with His eye upon us, as one who is watching the road with us.

pool.theme: Sing to Him a new song
pool.reflection: Praise, the psalm says, “is fitting for the straight.” It suits them. So bring the lyre and the ten strings, play well, and shout for joy. A new song is called for because His kindness did not stop with yesterday's, and the old words alone cannot hold what He has done since.

Nations take counsel and peoples lay plans, and Yahuah brings them to nothing. One counsel is left standing through every generation, “the plans of His heart.” So the baruk nation is not the strongest one. It is the one whose Aluahim is Yahuah, the people He chose as His own inheritance.

The psalm closes with a people waiting: “Our being has longed for Yahuah.” Their heart rejoices in Him because they have trusted in His qadash Name. The last line is a prayer that asks for kindness in the meantime: “Let Your kindness, O Yahuah, be upon us, even as we wait for You.”

The psalm's ancient title sets it when Dawiḏ escaped from Aḇimeleḵ by pretending to be mad. “This poor one cried out and Yahuah heard him” is his own story. So he does not argue anyone into trust; he invites: “Oh, taste and see that Yahuah is good.” The mal'ak of Yahuah encamps around those who fear Him.

The psalm does not say the righteous are spared: “Many are the evils of the righteous.” It says where Yahuah is when the heart breaks and the ruach is crushed. He is near. He hears the cry, and He delivers out of them all, however many they are.

pool.theme: In Your light we see light
pool.reflection: Dawiḏ reaches for the largest things he knows to measure with: kindness as high as the shamayim, righteousness like the mighty mountains, right-rulings like the great deep. Then he comes in close, to the shadow of His wings and the river of His pleasures. “With You is the fountain of life.”

This psalm is written for the one who is fretting over evil-doers who prosper. Its answer is a set of plain things to do instead: trust in Yahuah and do good, dwell and feed on steadfastness, delight yourself in Him, commit your way to Him. The outcome is His: “He does it.”

pool.theme: Though he falls, he is not cast down
pool.reflection: The psalm does not promise that the man whose steps Yahuah orders will never fall. It says what happens when he does: “he is not cast down, for Yahuah is supporting his hand.” A fall and a ruin are different things, and the difference is whose hand is holding.

pool.theme: He set my feet upon a rock
pool.reflection: “I waited, waited for Yahuah”: the word is doubled because the wait was long. Then come the things He did. He inclined, heard, drew Dawiḏ out of the muddy clay, set his feet on a rock, put a new song in his mouth. The song is for others too: “Many do see it and fear, and trust in Yahuah.”

pool.theme: Why are you depressed, O my being?
pool.reflection: The sons of Qoraḥ sing honestly here. In the same breath there is a song in the night and the question, “Why have You forgotten me?” The psalmist does not wait for the feeling to pass. He speaks to his own being: “Wait for Aluahim: for I shall yet thank Him.”

pool.theme: A help in distress, soon found
pool.reflection: The psalm pictures the worst it can think of, the earth reeling and mountains toppling into the heart of the seas, and says, “Therefore we do not fear.” The reason is not that such things cannot happen. It is that Aluahim is our refuge and strength, a help “soon found.”

Nations rage and reigns topple in this psalm, and into that noise Aluahim speaks: “Be still and know that I am Aluahim.” It is a command to stop. He will be exalted in the earth whether we strive or not. The closing line says who He is to us: Yahuah of hosts “is with us.”

pool.theme: Call upon Me in the day of distress
pool.reflection: Yahuah has just said He has no need of bulls and goats, since every beast of the forest is His. What He asks for is thanksgiving, vows kept, and a call in the day of trouble. The order He sets is this: you call, “let Me rescue you,” and you esteem Him.

pool.theme: Create in me a clean heart
pool.reflection: By its ancient title, Dawiḏ prayed this after Nathan the naḇi came to him about Bathsheḇa. He does not ask to have his old heart mended. He uses the word for what only Aluahim does: “Create.” And he asks for the thing sin had cost him: “Restore to me the joy of Your deliverance.”

Dawiḏ had been betrayed by a close friend, a man he used to walk with to the House of Aluahim. He leaves the men of blood and deceit to Aluahim, and he tells us what to do with the weight: cast it on Yahuah, who sustains. His own last word is, “But I, I trust in You.”

pool.theme: In the day I am afraid
pool.reflection: The psalm's ancient title sets it when the Philistines seized Dawiḏ in Gath. He does not claim to feel no fear. “In the day I am afraid, I trust in You.” Fear is the occasion for the trusting. By the next line it has become a question with an obvious answer: “What could flesh do to me?”

pool.theme: You put my tears into Your bottle
pool.reflection: Dawiḏ is a wanderer and believes every step of it has been counted. His tears are kept, written in a book. From that he draws one certainty, “This I know, because Aluahim is for me.” The refrain returns stronger than before, now with the Name: “In Yahuah, whose Word I praise.”

The psalm's ancient title puts Dawiḏ in a cave, hiding from Sha’ul, and from inside it he is thinking about the nations hearing his song. His circumstances are the size of a cave. His view of Yahuah's kindness is the size of the sky: “great up to the shamayim, and Your truth unto the clouds.”

By its ancient title this belongs to the night Sha’ul sent men to watch the house and kill Dawiḏ. They prowled around it like dogs at evening. “And I,” says Dawiḏ, “I sing of Your power.” Morning came and he was still alive to sing it. He calls Yahuah by a name he had earned the right to use: “my strong tower.”

pool.theme: The rock that is higher than I
pool.reflection: Dawiḏ calls “from the end of the earth,” with a faint heart. He does not ask for strength to climb. He asks to be led to a rock higher than himself, somewhere he could not reach alone. He has been there before: “You have been my refuge.”

Dawiḏ speaks to his own being: find rest “in Aluahim alone.” The word “alone” comes again and again in this psalm, because rest shared out among other supports is not rest. Then he turns to the people: trust in Him at all times, “pour out your heart before Him.”

pool.theme: Your kindness is better than life
pool.reflection: By its ancient title a psalm of Dawiḏ in the wilderness of Yahuḏah, a dry and thirsty land without water, and it is not water he says he is thirsty for. He has seen Yahuah's power and esteem in the Qodash and wants Him. “Your kindness is better than life,” so he lifts his hands and blesses.

Still in the wilderness, Dawiḏ lies awake and uses the hours: “I meditate on You in the night watches.” What he remembers is help already given. Then two hands are described. His own being clings to Yahuah, and underneath that, “Your right hand did uphold me.”

pool.theme: You crown the year with Your goodness
pool.reflection: This is a harvest psalm. The rain that softens the ridges and the grain standing in the furrows are spoken of as visits from Aluahim: “You have visited the earth and watered it.” Every meal has this behind it. The year wears His goodness like a crown.

pool.theme: What He has done for my being
pool.reflection: “Come, hear,” the psalmist says, and what follows is testimony: I called, and Aluahim heard. He is honest that wickedness cherished in the heart would have stopped the prayer. The psalm ends in thanks that neither thing was taken away, “my prayer, nor His kindness from me.”

pool.theme: That Your way be known on earth
pool.reflection: This prayer takes up the berakah of the kohanim, “cause His face to shine upon us,” and then says what the blessing is for: so that His way is known on earth and His deliverance among all nations. Yasharal is blessed so the peoples may praise Him.

He rides through the deserts and His Name is Yah, and the psalm at once tells us what the great Rider is occupied with: the fatherless, the widow, the lonely, the bound. From His qadash dwelling Aluahim makes homes for those who have none and brings prisoners out.

pool.theme: Day by day He bears our burden
pool.reflection: The berakah here is for something daily. He “bears our burden” each day as it comes. Twice He is called the Al of deliverance, and the last line reaches as far as it is possible to go: to Yahuah the Master “belong escapes from death.”

pool.theme: When I am old and grey
pool.reflection: An old man is praying. He was taught by Aluahim from his youth and has declared His wonders ever since. He asks not to be forsaken now, and gives his reason: there is a generation coming that has not yet heard of His strength. He wants to live long enough to tell them.

Asaph nearly lost his footing envying the prosperity of the wrong, until he went into the Qodash of Al. This is what he came out saying. He is held by the right hand, led by counsel, and afterward received to esteem. Flesh and heart waste away, “but Aluahim is the rock of my heart.”

pool.theme: I remember the deeds of Yah
pool.reflection: Asaph could not sleep and asked whether Aluahim had forgotten to show chen. He does not feel his way out of it. He remembers his way out: “I remember Your wonders of old.” He sets himself to meditate and to talk of what Aluahim has done, and the question changes to “Who is a great Al like Aluahim?”

pool.theme: How lovely are Your dwelling places
pool.reflection: The sons of Qoraḥ sing of longing for the courts of Yahuah until heart and flesh cry out. They even envy the sparrow and the swallow that nest near His mizbe'achot. What they want is not the building but “the living Al.” Baruk are those who dwell in His house.

One day in His courts is better than a thousand elsewhere, and the psalmist would rather keep the door there than live comfortably among the wrong. Yahuah gives chen and esteem. And there is this promise to hold: “He withholds no good matter from those who walk blamelessly.”

pool.theme: He speaks shalom to His people
pool.reflection: The psalmist stops asking and listens: “Let me hear what Al Yahuah speaks.” What He speaks is shalom to His people, with a warning not to turn back to folly. Then four things that men find hard to hold together meet in Him: kindness and truth, righteousness and shalom.

Dawiḏ calls himself poor and needy in this prayer, and everything he asks rests on what Yahuah is: good, ready to forgive, great in kindness to all who call. So he calls, in the day of his distress, with a confidence that is not in himself: “For You answer me.”

Dawiḏ asks to be taught the way and to walk in it, and then prays for the thing that makes walking possible: “Unite my heart to fear Your Name.” A divided heart goes two ways at once. With a whole one he can praise “with all my heart.”

The psalmist sings of the kindnesses of Yahuah and His oath to Dawiḏ. Later this same psalm grieves that the throne seems cast down. So the opening is a choice made in a hard season: “With my mouth I make known Your trustworthiness.” It is established in the shamayim, above what he can see.

The psalm's ancient title calls it a prayer of Mosheh, the man of Aluahim, who never had a settled home: a palace not his own, then Miḏyan, then forty years of tents. “Yahuah, You have been our refuge in all generations.” Before the mountains were born, He was Al. The home was a Person.

pool.theme: Teach us to number our days
pool.reflection: Mosheh watched a generation die in the wilderness, and he asks for the wisdom that comes from knowing our days are counted. Then he asks for more than soberness: “Satisfy us in the morning with Your kindness,” so that short days can still be sung through with joy.

pool.theme: The secret place of the Most High
pool.reflection: Four names are used in two verses, Most High, Almighty, Yahuah, my Aluahim, and one man who dwells under them all. He does not visit the shadow of the Almighty; he abides there. And he says so aloud, to Yahuah: “My refuge and my stronghold, my Aluahim, in whom I trust!”

pool.theme: He commands His mal'akim concerning you
pool.reflection: The promise is made to the one who has made Yahuah his dwelling place. The adversary quoted these lines to Yahusha in the wilderness, urging Him to throw Himself down, and Yahusha answered that you do not try Yahuah your Aluahim. The guarding is for the one who dwells, not the one who tests.

pool.theme: Because he has known My Name
pool.reflection: At the end of the psalm Yahuah speaks for Himself, and He says “I” again and again: I deliver him, I set him on high, I answer him, I am with him in distress. Two things are said of the man: he cleaves to Him in love, and he has known His Name.

pool.theme: It is good to give thanks
pool.reflection: The psalm's ancient title calls it a song for the Shabbath day. It gives the day its bookends: His kindness declared in the morning and His trustworthiness each night. Between them, strings and the harp, and the reason for the music: “You have made me rejoice with Your work.”

pool.theme: Still bearing fruit in old age
pool.reflection: The wrong spring up like grass, earlier in this psalm, and are gone. The righteous grow like a palm and a cedar, slowly and for a long time, because of where they are planted: in the House of Yahuah. Even in old age they are fresh and green, and their fruit says that Yahuah is straight.

pool.theme: When I said, “My foot has slipped”
pool.reflection: The psalmist remembers how near he came: without Yahuah's help he would soon have “settled in silence.” He said his foot was slipping, and found kindness holding him up as he said it. And when anxious thoughts multiplied within him, “Your comforts delighted my being.”

“Come, let us sing.” It is a call to do this together, to come before His face with thanksgiving and a shout. The psalm goes on to warn of hearts hardened in the wilderness. Thanksgiving sung in company is one of the ways a heart is kept soft.

pool.theme: Declare His esteem among the nations
pool.reflection: The same song was sung when the ark was brought up to Yahrushalayim. “Sing to Yahuah, all the earth”: the praise of Yasharal's Aluahim was never meant to stay inside Yasharal. His deliverance is to be proclaimed from day to day, because He is great “above all mighty ones.”

pool.theme: Light is sown for the righteous
pool.reflection: To love Yahuah is to hate evil; the psalm does not let the two be separated. Then a farmer's picture: light is “sown” for the righteous, and gladness for the upright in heart. It is in the ground already. What has been sown comes up in its season.

Yahuah has not kept His deliverance private. He showed His righteousness openly, “before the eyes of the nations,” and it came from remembering His kindness and trustworthiness to the house of Yasharal. So the whole earth is called to answer with a shout and a song.

A psalm of thanksgiving for all the earth. In the middle of the shouting and singing there is one thing to know: Yahuah is Aluahim, “He has made us and we are His.” We are the sheep of His pasture. The gates are entered with thanks, because His kindness is everlasting.

pool.theme: Do not forget all His dealings
pool.reflection: Dawiḏ speaks to his own being and tells it to bless Yahuah, and not to forget. Then he lists what forgetting would lose: crookednesses forgiven, diseases healed, a life redeemed from destruction, a crown of kindness and compassion, desire satisfied with good. Praise begins with remembering.

pool.theme: As far as east is from west
pool.reflection: Dawiḏ quotes what Yahuah proclaimed to Mosheh on the mountain: compassionate, showing chen, patient, great in kindness. Then he measures it. The kindness is as high as the shamayim above the earth. The transgressions are removed as far as east is from west, two points that never meet.

pool.theme: He remembers that we are dust
pool.reflection: A father knows what his children are made of and does not ask more than they can bear. Yahuah knows how we are formed. Our days are like a flower the ruach blows over. Against that brevity stands one thing “from everlasting to everlasting”: His kindness on those who fear Him.

This comes at the end of a long psalm about springs, cedars, wild goats, the moon, the great sea. Having looked at all Yahuah's works, the singer settles what he will do with his own days: “I sing to Yahuah as long as I live.” His meditation on Him is sweet.

The psalm goes on to retell the whole story from Aḇraham to the land. It begins with what a people who have such a story should do: give thanks, call on His Name, make known His deeds, sing. And it says who has cause for joy: “those seeking Yahuah.”

pool.theme: Let the redeemed of Yahuah say so
pool.reflection: The psalm opens with the refrain Yasharal sang at the House: He is good, His kindness is everlasting. Then it says whose business it is to say so, those He has redeemed from the hand of the adversary and gathered from east, west, north and south. Redemption is meant to be spoken.

pool.theme: He has satisfied the longing being
pool.reflection: In the psalm these words follow travellers lost in a wasteland, hungry, thirsty and fainting, who cried out and were led by a straight way to a city. It is their thanksgiving. He “has filled the hungry being with goodness,” and those who have been filled owe Him thanks for His kindness.

pool.theme: He caused the storm to be still
pool.reflection: These are the seafarers of the psalm, reeling on a ship with all their skill swallowed up. “Then they cry out to Yahuah.” He hushes the waves and brings them to the haven they longed for. The taught ones in the boat on Kinnereth saw Yahusha do exactly this.

“My heart is steadfast,” Dawiḏ says, and because it is settled he can sing. He does not wait for morning to rouse him; with harp and lyre he rouses the morning. His reason is as large as it can be: Yahuah's kindness is “great above the shamayim.”

pool.theme: He has made His wonders to be remembered
pool.reflection: “I thank Yahuah with all my heart,” and he does it in company, in the qahal. The works of Yahuah are great, and they are searched out by all who delight in them. He does not want them forgotten. He has made His wonders to be remembered.

pool.theme: Not afraid of an evil report
pool.reflection: This is the man who fears Yahuah and delights in His commands. The psalm does not say bad news never reaches him. It says he is not afraid of it, because his heart was fixed beforehand: “steadfast, trusting in Yahuah.” The trust was settled before the report arrived.

pool.theme: He is their help and their shield
pool.reflection: The psalm has just described idols with mouths that do not speak and hands that do not feel. Yahuah is the opposite: “Yahuah has remembered us.” He blesses the house of Yasharal, the house of Aharon, and all who fear Him, and no one is left out for being small: “the small and the great.”

“I love Yahuah,” and the reason is simple: He heard my voice. The picture is of someone bending down to catch what a weak voice is saying. Having been heard once, the psalmist settles the matter for the rest of his life: “I shall call throughout my days.”

pool.theme: Return to your rest, O my being
pool.reflection: He was brought low, and Yahuah saved him. So he speaks to his own being, which is still unsettled after the danger has passed, and tells it to go home: “Return to your rest, O my being, for Yahuah has treated you well.” Being from death, eyes from tears, feet from falling.

pool.theme: What shall I return to Yahuah?
pool.reflection: The question has no adequate answer; “all His bounties are upon me.” So the psalmist does the only fitting things. He lifts up the cup of deliverance, calls on the Name, and keeps his vows in front of the people. He answers the gift by receiving it gladly and saying so publicly.

The shortest psalm has the widest reach. Every nation and all peoples are called to praise Yahuah, and Sha’ul quotes it in Romans to show the gentiles were always in view. Two reasons are given: His kindness is mighty over us, and His truth is everlasting. HalleluYah.

pool.theme: Yah answered me in a broad place
pool.reflection: He called from a tight place, which is what the word for distress means, and was answered with room. “Yahuah is on my side; I do not fear what man does to me.” From that he draws the plain conclusion: it is better to take refuge in Yahuah than to trust in man.

pool.theme: Let me not die, but live
pool.reflection: The first line is from the song at the sea: “Yah is my strength and song.” The psalmist has been pushed hard and expected to fall. Now rejoicing is heard in the tents of the righteous. He knows what the rest of his life is for: to “declare the works of Yah.”

The builders looked the stone over and threw it aside, and Yahuah made it the chief corner-stone. Yahusha said these words of Himself. “This was from Yahuah, it is marvellous in our eyes.” That is the day the psalm calls us to rejoice in, the day of what He has done.

How does a young man keep his path clean? By guarding it according to the word. The psalmist seeks Yahuah with all his heart and still asks not to stray. He does not trust himself. He stores the word inside, where it will be when he needs it.

pool.theme: Your word has given me life
pool.reflection: He reminds Yahuah of the word He Himself gave, the word that taught him to wait. In his affliction he has nothing new to show for the waiting. His comfort is that the word is still there, and it has kept him alive.

“Forever, O Yahuah, Your word stands firm in the shamayim.” It is fixed where nothing on earth can reach to alter it. The proof he offers is underfoot: He established the earth, “and it stands.” His trustworthiness runs to all generations, including this one.

The word is sweet to him, sweeter than honey, and it gives him understanding enough to hate every false way. Then the well-known line. A lamp for the feet lights the next step on the path. It is enough to walk by.

pool.theme: The opening of Your words gives light
pool.reflection: “Your witnesses are wonders,” so he keeps them. The light comes when the words are opened, as when a door is opened on a dark room. It is given to “the simple,” to anyone who will come and have the word opened to them.

Those who love the Torah of Yahuah have great shalom, “and for them there is no stumbling-block.” The psalmist does not treat waiting and doing as rivals. He has waited for Yahuah's deliverance and has done His commands, both at once.

pool.theme: He who watches over you does not slumber
pool.reflection: This is a song of ascents, sung on the road up to Yahrushalayim. The traveller looks at the hills ahead and asks where help comes from. It comes from the Maker of the hills. His footing is kept by One who “neither slumbers nor sleeps.”

pool.theme: Your going out and your coming in
pool.reflection: “Guard” is the word of this psalm; it comes again and again. Yahuah is your guard and your shade, by day and by night. He guards your being, and He guards the ordinary movements of a life, the going out in the morning and the coming home, “now and forever.”

“If Yahuah had not been for us,” the psalm begins, and this is how it ends. The bird did not free itself. The snare was broken, and we escaped. The conclusion is one every generation of Yasharal has had to learn: “Our help is in the Name of Yahuah.”

Two pictures from one landscape. Those who trust in Yahuah are like Mount Tsiyon, which does not move. And as the hills stand round the city on every side, “so Yahuah surrounds His people.” Pilgrims sang this while looking at those very hills.

When Yahuah turns back the captivity of Tsiyon it will seem too good to be real. Mouths will fill with laughter, and even the gentiles will say, “Yahuah has done great deeds for them.” The people take up the same words for themselves and are glad.

The sower goes out weeping and goes on sowing anyway. Seed carried in tears is still seed. The psalm promises the same person a return journey with arms full: he “shall indeed come in with rejoicing, bearing his sheaves.”

pool.theme: If Yahuah does not build the house
pool.reflection: A song of ascents, of Shelomoh, who built the greatest House in Yasharal. Building and guarding are good work, and without Yahuah both are in vain. So is anxious toil stretched from early morning to late at night. “He gives His beloved sleep.”

pool.theme: Baruk are all who fear Yahuah
pool.reflection: The berakah here is ordinary: you work, and you eat what your hands have made. “Be baruk and let it be well with you.” The psalm promises it to all who fear Yahuah and walk in His ways, which is two things together, reverence and a way of living.

pool.theme: More than those watching for morning
pool.reflection: A song from the depths. He waits for Yahuah the way a watchman on the wall waits for morning, and says it twice. The night is long, and the dawn is certain. Then he tells Yasharal why to wait: with Yahuah there is kindness, “and with Him is much redemption.”

Dawiḏ has stopped reaching for matters too great and too wondrous for him. He has calmed his being like a weaned child with its mother, one that no longer cries for milk and is content simply to be held. From that quiet he says to all Yasharal: wait for Yahuah.

Unity among brothers is compared to two things that come down from above: the anointing oil running down Aharon's beard, and the dew of Ḥermon falling on Tsiyon. It is given, not manufactured. And it is where Yahuah commands the berakah, “life forever.”

pool.theme: Do not forsake the works of Your hands
pool.reflection: Yahuah is exalted and He looks on the humble; the proud He knows from a distance. Dawiḏ walks “in the midst of distress” and is revived there. He is sure Yahuah will finish what concerns him, and prays on that ground: we are the works of His hands.

pool.theme: You have searched me and know me
pool.reflection: Dawiḏ is known completely: when he sits and rises, his thoughts from far off, his path, the word not yet on his tongue. He says it with wonder and no fear. The One who knows all of him is the One he is speaking to, by Name.

pool.theme: Where would I go from Your Ruach?
pool.reflection: Dawiḏ tries every direction: up into the shamayim, down to the grave, east on the wings of the morning, west beyond the sea. He is not escaping. In the farthest place he finds a hand already there: “Your hand would lead me, and Your right hand hold me.”

Before anyone saw him, Dawiḏ was seen, covered in his mother's womb by the One who formed his inmost parts. His response is thanks: “Wondrous are Your works, and my being knows it well.” What Yahuah made with that care, He has not stopped caring for.

The psalm began, “You have searched me.” It ends by asking for it. Having seen how fully he is known, Dawiḏ invites the search, and asks that whatever false way is found be dealt with. “Lead me in the way everlasting.”

pool.theme: Set a guard for my mouth
pool.reflection: Dawiḏ asks that his prayer rise like the incense and his lifted hands be like the evening offering. Then he asks for a watchman at the door of his lips. He wants the same mouth that prays to be kept in what it says to people.

pool.theme: Let me hear Your kindness in the morning
pool.reflection: Dawiḏ is pursued and his ruach is faint within him. He asks for four things before the day begins: to hear kindness, to know the way to walk, to be delivered, to be taught. And he asks who will lead him: “Let Your good Ruach lead me in the land of straightness.”

Dawiḏ again takes up the words proclaimed to Mosheh: showing chen, compassionate, patient, great in kindness. Then he widens them past Yasharal and past mankind: “Yahuah is good to all, and He has compassion on all His works.” Everything He made is within reach of it.

His reign is everlasting, and look what the Sovereign does with it: He supports all who are falling and raises all who are bowed down. Every living thing looks to Him, and He feeds them in season. The whole creation eats from an opened hand.

pool.theme: Near to all who call upon Him
pool.reflection: The condition is small and searching: “all who call upon Him in truth.” No fine words are needed, only honest ones. To those who fear Him the psalm promises three things in a row. He does their desire, He hears their cry, and He saves them.

The psalm has just said not to trust in princes, whose plans perish the day their breath leaves. Then it lists what the Maker of the shamayim and earth is doing: right-ruling for the oppressed, bread for the hungry, release for the bound, sight for the blind. He guards the stranger, the fatherless and the widow.

Two verses stand side by side on purpose. He binds up the wounds of the broken-hearted. He appoints the number of the stars and gives every one a name. The power that orders the shamayim is the power that attends to one hurt person, and “there is no limit to His understanding.”

pool.theme: In those who wait for His kindness
pool.reflection: The strength of a war-horse and the legs of a strong man do not impress Yahuah. What He takes pleasure in can be found in the weakest person: fear of Him, and waiting for His kindness. It takes no strength at all to give Him what He delights in.

pool.theme: He commanded and they were created
pool.reflection: Sun, moon, stars of light, the shamayim of shamayim and the waters above them are all called to praise the Name of Yahuah. Their reason is their existence: He commanded, and they were. He set them a law they do not pass beyond. Their keeping to their courses is their praise.

pool.theme: Yahuah takes pleasure in His people
pool.reflection: Here is praise with dancing, tambourine and lyre, and the reason is given: “Yahuah takes pleasure in His people.” He is glad of them. He adorns the meek with deliverance, as one dresses someone for a celebration.

The book of Tehillim ends on one word said over and over. Praise Him in His Qodash and in His mighty expanse, for what He has done and for who He is, with ram's horn, harp, strings, flutes and cymbals. The only requirement left at the end is breath. HalleluYah.

The chapter begins with a son told to cry out for understanding and search for it like silver. Here is why the search is not hopeless: wisdom is given, and it comes “out of His mouth.” The same Giver is a shield to those walking blamelessly and guards the way of His kind ones.

pool.theme: Write them on the tablet of your heart
pool.reflection: A father asks his son to hold on to two things, kindness and truth: bind them around your neck, write them on your heart. They are the pair Yahuah proclaimed of Himself to Mosheh. The son who keeps them finds chen “in the eyes of Aluahim and man.”

pool.theme: Lean not on your own understanding
pool.reflection: Trust with “all your heart” leaves no part held back to lean on your own understanding. The proverb does not say to stop thinking. It says where the weight goes. “Know Him in all your ways,” not only the large decisions, and the straightening of the paths is His doing.

pool.theme: The first-fruits of all your increase
pool.reflection: Yahuah is esteemed with goods as well as with words, and from the first of the increase, before the rest is spent. That is how Yasharal brought their first-fruits. The proverb pairs it with full storehouses, because the one who gives first has said who the harvest came from.

The proverb asks a son not to despise discipline or grow weary of reproof, and gives the reason that changes how it feels: it comes “as a father the son whom he delights in.” The letter to the Iḇrim quotes these lines to people worn down by hardship.

The man who finds Wisdom is called baruk, and the proverb reckons it like a merchant: better gain than silver, better increase than fine gold, more precious than rubies. Then it runs out of comparisons: “all your delights are not comparable to her.”

“Sudden dread” is the kind that arrives without warning, and the proverb says not to be afraid of it. The reason is not that nothing sudden will come. It is where Yahuah stands when it does: “at your side,” guarding your foot from being caught.

A father asks for his son's ears, eyes and heart, because his words are “life to those who find them.” Then the charge above all others: watch over your heart with all diligence. Everything a person does flows out from there, as water flows from a spring.

This is counsel for walking: eyes straight ahead, the path considered, no turning to the right or the left. Most stumbling starts with looking aside. The last line makes it plain what kind of path is meant: “Turn your foot away from evil.”

Wisdom herself is speaking, and she pictures the one she calls baruk: someone at her gates every day, waiting at the posts of her doors as a servant waits for the house to open. The word is “daily.” Wisdom is heard by those who keep turning up to listen.

A wise person can still be taught and becomes wiser; that is one of the marks of being wise. And the starting point is named: “The fear of Yahuah is the beginning of wisdom.” To know the Qadash One is what the proverb means by understanding.

The mouth of the righteous is “a fountain of life”; people are better for having been near it. Hatred goes looking for a quarrel and stirs one up. Love does the reverse with an offence and covers it. Kĕpha quotes this line when he tells believers to love one another fervently.

There are riches that come with sorrow attached. The berakah of Yahuah makes rich, “and He adds no pain with it.” The verses that follow set two men side by side: what the wrong one fears comes upon him, “but the desire of the righteous is granted.”

Pride arrives first and shame follows behind it; the proverb puts them in that order. Wisdom keeps company with the humble. For the straight there is a guide that goes everywhere with them: their own integrity.

pool.theme: He who waters is also watered
pool.reflection: The arithmetic is strange on purpose. One man scatters and has more; another holds back more than is right and comes to poverty. “The generous being is enriched.” The proverb's picture is of water: the one who gives others drink does not go dry.

pool.theme: The tongue of the wise is healing
pool.reflection: Rash words go in like a sword. The proverb sets against them a tongue that heals, and says something about how long each kind of speech lasts: “The lip of truth is established forever, but a lying tongue is but for a moment.”

pool.theme: A good word makes him glad
pool.reflection: Anxiety weighs a heart down, the proverb says, and it names something that lifts it: “a good word.” It costs the speaker very little. The next line widens it: the righteous is a guide to his neighbour. Other people's roads are partly in our keeping.

pool.theme: A longing come true is a tree of life
pool.reflection: The proverb admits that a hope drawn out makes the heart sick. It also knows the other side: a longing fulfilled is “a tree of life.” Meanwhile there is something to drink from while waiting: “The Torah of the wise is a fountain of life.”

pool.theme: A place of refuge for His children
pool.reflection: The fear of Yahuah is usually spoken of as a beginning. Here it is a shelter: “strong trust,” and a refuge that reaches to a man's children. It is also “a fountain of life,” turning a person aside from the snares of death before he steps in them.

pool.theme: He who is patient has great understanding
pool.reflection: In this translation the quick-tempered man is “short of ruach,” short of breath. The patient one has room to understand before he answers. The second proverb looks inward: a heart at rest gives life to the whole body, while envy works like rot in the bones.

pool.theme: A soft answer turns away wrath
pool.reflection: Four proverbs about the tongue, with one in the middle that explains why speech matters: “The eyes of Yahuah are in every place,” watching the evil and the good. A soft answer turns wrath aside, and a healing tongue is called a tree of life. He hears which kind we choose.

What is in the heart shows on the face. The proverb is honest that the days of the afflicted are hard. It also says gladness of heart is “a continual feast,” one that does not depend on what is on the table.

Two “better than” sayings weigh what is on the table against who is around it. A little with the fear of Yahuah is better than treasure with trouble. A meal of vegetables where love is beats the fatted calf served with hatred. Both proverbs prize the company over the food.

A man arranges his thoughts, but the answer of the tongue is from Yahuah. His ways look clean to him, but Yahuah weighs the ruchot, the motives behind them. So the counsel is to roll the work itself onto Him: “and your plans shall be established.”

When a man's ways please Yahuah, even his enemies are brought to shalom with him. A little with righteousness is better than a large income without right-ruling. And the proverb many know by heart: the heart plans the way, “but Yahuah establishes his steps.”

pool.theme: Baruk is he who trusts in Yahuah
pool.reflection: Two things are joined that we tend to separate. Acting wisely concerning the Word finds good, and trusting in Yahuah is called baruk. The next line adds a note on teaching: it is “sweetness of lips,” a pleasant way of speaking, that increases learning.

pool.theme: Pleasant words are like a honeycomb
pool.reflection: Speech begins in the heart; the wise heart gives discretion to the mouth. And kind words do more than please. The proverb says they reach the whole person: “sweet to the being and healing to the bones.”

pool.theme: He who rules over his ruach
pool.reflection: The proverb sets two conquerors side by side and prefers the quiet one. To be patient is better than to be mighty, and ruling your own ruach is a greater thing than taking a city. Even the lot cast into the lap falls as Yahuah decides.

pool.theme: The Name of Yahuah is a strong tower
pool.reflection: Two places of safety are set next to each other. The righteous run into the Name of Yahuah and are safe. The rich man has his wealth, which is a high wall “in his own imagination.” One tower is real. The last verse says what goes before each end: a haughty heart, or humility.

pool.theme: Death and life are in the power of the tongue
pool.reflection: A man lives on the harvest of his own words, the proverb says; he is filled with what his lips produce. That is true for good and for ill: “Death and life are in the power of the tongue.” Whoever loves to use it will eat its fruit.

Listen to counsel and accept discipline while it can still do you good, so that you are wise at the end. The second proverb tells why humility about our plans is only realistic. The heart holds many of them. One counsel stands.

pool.theme: He who pursues righteousness and kindness
pool.reflection: The word is “pursues.” Righteousness and kindness are to be chased, and the one who does finds more than he was after: “life, righteousness and esteem.” The third proverb brings it down to the mouth. Whoever guards his tongue guards his life from distresses.

A good name is worth more than great riches, and chen more than silver and gold. Then rich and poor are stood side by side: “Yahuah is the Maker of them all.” Whatever separates them in the street, they meet as His workmanship.

Humility and the fear of Yahuah come with a reward: riches, esteem and life. The way of the perverse is full of thorns and snares. Between those two roads stands a child, and someone must set him on the right one early. What he learns then stays with him: “even when he is old.”

Envy of sinners is treated as a matter of where the heart spends its day. The alternative is to be “in the fear of Yahuah all day long.” The reason given is the long view: “For certain, there is a hereafter.” What the envied have now is not the end of the matter.

pool.theme: Wisdom is thus to your being
pool.reflection: A father tells his son to eat honey because it is good, and then makes it a lesson. Wisdom is to the being what honey is to the mouth. Find it and “there is a future, and your expectancy is not cut off.”

pool.theme: A word spoken at the right time
pool.reflection: The proverb is about timing. The right word at the right moment is like apples of gold in settings of silver. Even reproof can be an ornament when it comes from someone wise, provided it meets “an ear that hears.” Both the speaker and the listener have a part.

Bread for a hungry enemy, water for a thirsty one. Sha’ul quotes these lines in Romans where he says not to be overcome by evil but to overcome evil with good. The proverb leaves the outcome with Yahuah: “and Yahuah rewards you.”

An edge comes from another piece of iron, and a man is sharpened by the face of his friend, in his company. The one who tends the fig tree eats its fruit. And as water gives back a face, a man's heart shows what he is.
