Hiding transgression is one way of dealing with it, and the proverb says it does not prosper. There are two parts to the other way: confessing and forsaking. Whoever does both “finds compassion.” The hardened heart, in the next line, is the one that falls.

pool.theme: Every Word of Aloah is tried
pool.reflection: These are the words of Aḡur. The Word has been tested like metal in the fire and proved pure, and the One who spoke it is “a shield to those taking refuge in Him.” So nothing is to be added to it. A word that has been tried needs no improving.

Aḡur asks for two things before he dies: to be kept from falsehood, and to be given only his portion of bread. He fears being full enough to say “Who is Yahuah?” and poor enough to steal and dishonour the Name. It is the prayer Yahusha taught: daily bread.

pool.theme: The Torah of kindness on her tongue
pool.reflection: The capable wife of the last chapter is clothed in strength and splendour, and she can smile at the days ahead. When she opens her mouth it is with wisdom, and “on her tongue is the Torah of kindness.” What she teaches her household is kind.

These are her husband's words of praise, and then the book's closing verdict. Loveliness deceives and prettiness passes. What is praised is this: “a woman who fears Yahuah.” Mishle began by saying the fear of Yahuah is the beginning of knowledge, and it ends there too.

pool.theme: Baruk be the Name of Yahuah
pool.reflection: In one day Iyoḇ has lost his herds, his servants and his ten children. He tears his robe and shaves his head, so the grief is real, and then he falls to the ground and worships. “Yahuah has given and Yahuah has taken away.” He blesses the Name with empty hands.

pool.theme: I know that my Redeemer lives
pool.reflection: Iyoḇ says this from the ash heap, with his skin failing and his friends accusing him. He does not say he understands; he says he knows. His Redeemer lives and shall stand at the last over the dust, and “in my flesh I shall see Aloah,” with his own eyes and not a stranger's.

pool.theme: I would come forth as gold
pool.reflection: Iyoḇ has just said he cannot find Aluahim, forward or backward, left or right. Then comes the turn: “He knows the way that I take.” Being seen matters more than seeing. And what Iyoḇ has held on to through the trying is the words of His mouth, treasured above his daily portion.

pool.theme: When the morning stars sang together
pool.reflection: After thirty-five chapters of argument Yahuah answers Iyoḇ out of the whirlwind, and He answers with questions. Where were you when the foundations were laid and the corner-stone set? They do not explain the suffering. They show Iyoḇ how much there is that he was never asked to carry.

Iyoḇ never does receive the explanation he demanded. What he receives is Yahuah Himself, and it is enough: “I have heard of You by the hearing of the ear but now my eye sees You.” The matters were too marvellous for him, he says, and he lays his questions down.

pool.theme: Rise up, my love, and come away
pool.reflection: The beloved comes to the window and calls: the winter is past, the rain is over, flowers have appeared, the turtledove is heard. He says “come away” twice. Many in Yasharal have heard in this the voice of Yahuah calling His people out after a long cold season.

pool.theme: Love is as strong as death
pool.reflection: She asks to be set as a seal on his heart and on his arm, where it cannot be lost. Then the song says what love is: as strong as death, its flames “a flame of Yah.” Many waters cannot put it out. A whole household's wealth could not buy it.

Ruth is a Mo’aḇite widow with every reason to go home, and Na‛omi has told her to. Her answer binds her to a road, a people and a Name: “your people is my people and your Aluahim is my Aluahim.” She came into Yasharal, and into the line of Dawiḏ, by clinging.

pool.theme: Under whose wings you have come
pool.reflection: Bo‛az has heard what Ruth left behind and what she did for her mother-in-law. His berakah gives her a picture of where she now stands: under the wings of Yahuah Aluahim of Yasharal, where she came to seek refuge. What is done quietly in loyalty is seen, and He repays it.

This book is a lament over Yahrushalayim in ruins, and at its centre is this. “We have not been consumed,” because His compassions have not ended. They are new every morning. A man who has lost everything says what he has left: “Yahuah is my Portion … therefore I wait for Him!”

The lament goes on, and its counsel is quiet. Yahuah is good to those waiting for Him, to the being who seeks Him. “It is good – both to wait and to be silent, for the deliverance of Yahuah.” Among the ruins there was nothing else to do, and it was enough.

pool.theme: He does not cast off forever
pool.reflection: Three lines begin with “For,” each one a reason to wait. Yahuah does not cast off forever. Though He afflicted, He shows compassion according to the greatness of His kindnesses. And affliction is not what His heart is set on: “He has not afflicted from His heart.”

pool.theme: You drew near on the day I called
pool.reflection: He called from “the lowest pit,” and he was heard there. “You drew near on the day I called on You and You said, ‘Do not fear!’” Yahuah pleaded his case as an advocate does and redeemed his life.

The Preacher has looked hard at toil and at time. He concludes that Aluahim has made everything fitting in its time, and set the ages in men's hearts so they reach for more than they can find out. Meanwhile to eat, drink and enjoy the good of one's work “is a gift of Aluahim.”

The Preacher has just described a man alone, working without end and never asking whom he does it for. Against that he sets two together: a hand up after a fall, warmth at night, a stand against an attacker. “And a threefold cord is not readily broken.”

Go to the House of Aluahim to listen, the Preacher says, and watch your step on the way in. He gives the reason in a single line: “Aluahim is in the shamayim and you on earth.” Before Him a few words are enough.

The Preacher has stared at death and at how little anyone controls, and this is what he tells us to do about it: eat with joy, drink with a glad heart, wear white, do not go without oil. The reason is a striking one: “Aluahim has already approved your works.”

pool.theme: The conclusion of the entire matter
pool.reflection: After twelve chapters of “futility” the book ends by saying what is not futile: “Fear Aluahim and guard His commands, for this applies to all mankind.” Every work will be brought into right-ruling, even what is hidden. Nothing done turns out to have been meaningless.

pool.theme: For such a time as this
pool.reflection: Mordeḵai will not let Estĕr think the palace makes her safe, and he is certain of one thing: deliverance for the Yahuḏim will come, if not through her then “from another place.” The only open question is whether she will have a part in it. Her place was given to her for this day.

pool.theme: The joy of Yahuah is your strength
pool.reflection: The people had stood from daybreak hearing the Torah read, and they wept when they understood it. Neḥemyah and Ezra tell them the day is qadash: eat, drink, send portions to those who have nothing prepared. Grief over the Word is right, but it is not where the day ends.

The Lĕwites call the people to stand and bless, and their prayer starts at the beginning: the shamayim and their host, the earth, the seas, “and You give life to them all.” Before they confess anything about themselves they say who He is. That order is worth keeping.

Dawiḏ gave this psalm to be sung on the day the ark came to rest in Yahrushalayim. It is a string of commands for a glad people: give thanks, call upon His Name, make known His deeds, sing, boast in His Name. And the one to carry into ordinary days: “Seek His face continually.”

The people have just given gold, silver and stones for the House, willingly and in heaps. Dawiḏ's prayer makes sure no one mistakes who the giver is: greatness, power, riches and esteem all come “from Your presence.” They had only handed back what was already His.

Yahuah says this to Shelomoh by night, after the dedication of the House. It is spoken to “My people upon whom My Name is called,” and it asks four things of them: to humble themselves, pray, seek His face and turn from their evil ways. Then He hears, forgives and heals their land.

pool.theme: Baruk are the poor in ruach
pool.reflection: Yahusha sat down on the mountain and began with those the world passes over: the poor in ruach, the mourners, the meek, the hungry for righteousness. Each is called baruk and each is given a reason. The first and the last have the same one, in the present tense: “theirs is the reign of the shamayim.”

Yahusha says this to taught ones who were fishermen and villagers: “You are the light of the world.” A lamp is lit to be put on a lampstand. The good works are to be seen, and the praise is meant to go past the one who does them to “your Father who is in the shamayim.”

Love for a neighbour was written in the Torah; hatred for an enemy was something people had added. Yahusha takes the addition away. Love, bless, do good, pray for them, and you resemble your Father, who “makes His sun rise on the wicked and on the good.”

Yahusha gives a short prayer, and its order teaches. The Father's Name, His reign and His desire come first. Then our bread for today, our debts, our trials. It is “our” and “us” throughout; no one prays it alone. It closes with Him: the reign, the power and the esteem.

Treasure on earth has three enemies, moth, rust and thieves. Treasure in the shamayim has none. But Yahusha's concern is the heart more than the treasure, because the one follows the other: “where your treasure is, there your heart shall be also.”

pool.theme: Look at the birds of the shamayim
pool.reflection: “Because of this” points back: no one can serve two masters. The one who serves Aluahim is told not to worry about food or clothing. The birds neither sow nor reap, and “your heavenly Father does feed them.” Worry cannot add a cubit to anyone's span of life.

pool.theme: Seek first the reign of Aluahim
pool.reflection: What to eat, drink and wear are the questions the nations run after. Yahusha does not say these needs are unreal: “your heavenly Father knows that you need all these.” He gives them their place. First His reign and His righteousness, and all these are added.

Three commands and three promises, and then Yahusha says it again so no one thinks he is the exception: “everyone who asks receives.” In the verses that follow He gives the reason, which is the Father, who knows how to give good gifts.

pool.theme: How much more shall your Father
pool.reflection: No father hands his hungry son a stone. If fathers who are far from good know how to give, “how much more” the Father in the shamayim. From that Yahusha draws the rule for dealing with others: do to them what you wish done to you. “This is the Torah and the Naḇi'im.”

These are nearly the last words of the teaching on the mountain. Both houses in the parable meet the same rain, floods and ruchot. The difference is underneath, and Yahusha says what the rock is: hearing “these words of Mine” and doing them.

Yahusha looked at the crowds and what He felt was compassion, because they were weary and scattered. He told His taught ones what He saw, a great harvest and few workers. The first thing He asked of them was prayer to the Master of the harvest.

pool.theme: Not one of them falls without your Father
pool.reflection: Two sparrows cost a copper coin, about the cheapest thing in the market, and not one falls to the ground apart from the Father. The hairs of your head are numbered. Yahusha said this to men He was sending out among wolves, and concluded: “So do not fear.”

The invitation is to all who labour and are burdened, and the rest is Yahusha's own gift: “I shall give you rest.” He does not offer a life with no yoke. He offers His, alongside One who is “meek and humble in heart,” and says it is gentle.

Two short parables about the reign of the shamayim. One man stumbles on treasure in a field; another has searched for fine pearls all his life. Both sell everything they have. The first parable tells us how it felt: he did it “for joy.”

pool.theme: Whoever loses his life for My sake
pool.reflection: Kĕpha had just tried to talk Yahusha out of the suffering ahead. Yahusha answers all the taught ones: to come after Him is to deny yourself, take up your stake and follow. A life kept back is lost and a life given for His sake is found. “What shall a man give in exchange for his life?”

Where two or three are gathered in His Name, Yahusha is in their midst. Then Kĕpha asks the question that life together always raises: how often must I forgive my brother? He offers seven and thinks it generous. Yahusha's answer puts an end to counting.

pool.theme: Not to be served, but to serve
pool.reflection: Ya'aqoḇ and Yahuchanon had asked for the seats on His right and left, and the other ten were angry. Yahusha says the rulers of the nations lord it over them, “but it shall not be so among you.” Greatness among His people is measured by the Son of Aḏam, who gave His life as a ransom for many.

The Sovereign welcomes those on His right into a reign prepared for them from the foundation of the world. Then He lists what they did: food, drink, a welcome, clothing, visits to the sick and the imprisoned. They do not remember doing any of it for Him. He counts it as done to Himself.

The eleven met Him on a mountain in Galil, and some still doubted. He did not wait for the doubt to clear. All authority is His, so they are to go, make taught ones of all nations, immerse and teach. His presence is promised for every day of it, “until the end of the age.”

A father has brought his son to the taught ones and they could do nothing. He says to Yahusha, “if You are able.” Yahusha turns the “if” around. The man's cry is one of the most honest prayers in Scripture: “I believe Master, help my unbelief!” Yahusha healed the boy.

pool.theme: Let the little children come to Me
pool.reflection: The taught ones thought children were too small a matter for the Master and turned them away. Yahusha was “much displeased.” The reign of Aluahim belongs to such as these, and it is received the way a child receives. Then He took them in His arms and blessed them.

Kĕpha had pointed out the withered fig tree, and Yahusha spoke about prayer. Ask believing. Then comes a condition the taught ones may not have expected: “whenever you stand praying, if you hold whatever against anyone, forgive.” Belief and a grudge do not pray well together.

pool.theme: The first of all the commands
pool.reflection: A scribe asks which command is first, and Yahusha answers with the Shema: “Hear, O Yasharal, Yahuah our Aluahim, Yahuah is one.” Love for Him with heart, being, mind and strength is first. Love for your neighbour, from Wayyiqra, is second. “There is no other command greater than these.”

Miryam is a young woman from Natsareth carrying a child she has been told is the Son of the Most High. Her song is about Him: He looked on the low state of His servant, He who is mighty has done wonders, qadash is His Name. His compassion goes on “from generation to generation.”

The first to hear were shepherds keeping watch over their flock by night. The mal'ak tells them not to fear. A Saviour is born in the city of Dawiḏ, and the sign is a baby lying in a feeding trough. Then the host of the shamayim sings: esteem to Aluahim, and on earth shalom.

pool.theme: My eyes have seen Your deliverance
pool.reflection: Shim‛on was an old man in Yahrushalayim who had been told he would not see death before he saw the Mashiach of Yahuah. He takes the child in his arms and says he can go in shalom. He names what he is holding: “a light for the unveiling of the gentiles and the esteem of Your people Yasharal.”

Yahusha says this “to you who are hearing,” and gives four things to do, each harder to avoid than the last: love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, bless those who curse you, pray for those who insult you. Anyone can do the last one today.

pool.theme: As your Father also is compassionate
pool.reflection: The standard is the Father, who “is kind to the thankless and wicked ones.” So lend expecting nothing, do not judge, do not condemn, forgive, give. The measure we use is the measure that comes back, and Yahusha describes it filled the generous way: pressed down, shaken together, running over.

Martha was serving, and no one says the serving was wrong. Yahusha says her name twice and names her trouble: worried and troubled about many matters. Miryam sat at His feet and listened to His word. That is the good portion, “which shall not be taken away from her.”

Yahusha calls them a little flock; He knows how few and how small they are. The fear is answered by what the Father delights to do: “to give you the reign.” Whoever is being given a reign can afford to hold possessions loosely and give in kindness.

Tax collectors and sinners were drawing near to hear Him, and the Pharisees complained. Yahusha asks which of them, owning a hundred sheep, would not go after the one that is lost “until he finds it.” He carries it home on his shoulders. There is joy in the shamayim over one sinner who repents.

pool.theme: While he was still a long way off
pool.reflection: The son had rehearsed a speech and hoped to be taken on as a hired servant. His father saw him far off, which means he had been looking, and ran. The speech is cut short by a robe, a ring, sandals and a feast: “this son of mine was dead and is alive again.”

Two men went up to pray. The Pharisee thanked Aluahim that he was not like others. The tax collector stood far off, would not lift his eyes, and asked for one thing. Yahusha says which of them went home declared right. The one who humbles himself is exalted.

pool.theme: To seek and to save what was lost
pool.reflection: Zakkai was a chief tax collector, rich and despised, and he had climbed a tree to see Yahusha. The crowd grumbled when Yahusha went to his house. Yahusha says that deliverance has come to it today, and that this is why He came: “to seek and to save what was lost.”

pool.theme: In the beginning was the Word
pool.reflection: Yahuchanon opens with the first words of Bereshith. The Word was with Aluahim, and all came to be through Him. In Him was life, and that life was the light of men. He writes the next line in the present tense: the light shines in the darkness, “and the darkness has not overcome it.”

To those who received Him He gave authority to become children of Aluahim, born of Aluahim and not of human desire. And the Word “pitched His tent among us,” as the Dwelling Place once stood in the midst of the camp. Those who saw Him saw esteem, “complete in chen and truth.”

Yahusha is speaking to Naḵdimon, a teacher of Yasharal who came by night. The love of Aluahim is measured by what He gave, His only brought-forth Son. The purpose of the sending is stated twice: that whoever believes should not perish, and that the world through Him might be saved.

pool.theme: A fountain of water springing up
pool.reflection: Yahusha is sitting by Ya'aqoḇ's well at noon, talking with a woman of Shomeron who came to draw. Everyone who drinks from the well thirsts again. The water He gives becomes a fountain inside a person, “springing up into everlasting life.” She left her jar and went to tell the town.

The woman asked which mountain was the right place to worship. Yahusha says the hour has come when the question is how, and not where: in ruach and truth. He adds something about the Father that is easy to pass over. He is seeking such worshippers.

pool.theme: I am the bread of life
pool.reflection: The crowd had eaten the loaves the day before and had come back for more. Yahusha offers Himself: whoever comes to Him will not hunger. To the one who is afraid to come He adds a promise: “the one who comes to Me I shall by no means cast out.”

On the last, great day of the Festival of Booths, when water from the pool of Shiloaḥ was poured out at the mizbe'ach, Yahusha stood and cried out: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to Me.” Yahuchanon explains that He spoke of the Ruach, whom those believing in Him were to receive.

pool.theme: The truth shall make you free
pool.reflection: This is said to people who already believed Him. Believing is the start; staying in His Word is what makes a taught one. The order is exact: stay, then know the truth, then be made free.

Yahusha calls Himself the door of the sheepfold, through which the sheep go in and out and find pasture. The thief comes to steal, slaughter and destroy. He came so that they might have life “beyond measure,” and He is the shepherd who lays down His life for the sheep.

pool.theme: No one shall snatch them out of My hand
pool.reflection: His sheep are known by three things: they hear His voice, He knows them, and they follow. He gives them everlasting life. Their safety is in two hands, His and His Father's, who “is greater than all.”

pool.theme: I am the resurrection and the life
pool.reflection: Martha's brother Al‛azar has been four days in the tomb. She believes in a resurrection at the last day. Yahusha tells her it is standing in front of her: “I am the resurrection and the life.” Then He asks her what He asks everyone who hears it: “Do you believe this?”

pool.theme: Unless a grain of wheat falls
pool.reflection: Some Greeks had asked to see Yahusha, and He answered by speaking of His death. A grain kept safe stays a single grain. Buried, it bears much fruit. He was speaking of Himself first, and then of anyone who serves Him: “where I am, there My servant also shall be.”

pool.theme: Walk while you have the light
pool.reflection: These are among His last words to the crowds before He hid Himself from them. The light is with them “yet a little while.” He gives them something to do while it is there: walk in it and believe in it, “so that you become sons of light.”

He had just washed their feet, and Yahuḏah had gone out into the night. The command to love was old. What renews it is the measure: “as I have loved you.” This is how others will know whose taught ones they are, by their love for one another.

pool.theme: Let not your heart be troubled
pool.reflection: He has just told them He is going away, that one of them will betray Him and that Kĕpha will deny Him. To those hearts He says, believe in Aluahim, believe also in Me. He goes to prepare a place and will come again, “that where I am, you might be too.”

T’oma says plainly what the others are thinking: we do not know where You are going, so how can we know the way? Yahusha does not hand him directions. The way to the Father is a Person: “I am the Way and the Truth and the Life.”

Love for Him shows in guarding His commands. And He does not leave them to do it alone. He will ask, and the Father will give another Helper, the Ruach of the Truth, to stay with them forever. The world cannot receive Him, “but you know Him, for He stays with you.”

pool.theme: My shalom I give to you
pool.reflection: Yahusha is about to be taken from them. The Ruach HaQadash will teach them and bring to mind all He said. And He leaves them something of His own: “My shalom.” It is not given as the world gives, so their hearts need not be troubled or afraid.

pool.theme: I am the vine, you are the branches
pool.reflection: A branch has one task, to stay in the vine. The fruit comes from that. Yahusha is plain about what happens otherwise: “without Me you are able to do naught.” The same sentence carries the promise that whoever stays in Him “bears much fruit.”

The love the Father has for the Son is the love the Son has for them, and they are told to stay in it by guarding His commands. He tells them this so that His joy may be in them and their joy be complete. Then He names love's furthest reach, which He was about to go to: laying down His life for His friends.

In a few hours they would be scattered and leave Him alone. He tells them beforehand, and without reproach. He wants them to have shalom in Him. He is honest about the world, “you have pressure,” and then gives the reason for courage: “I have overcome the world.”

This is Yahusha praying for His taught ones on the night He was betrayed. He does not ask for them to be taken out of the world. He asks that they be kept in it and set apart in the truth, and He says where the truth is found: “Your Word is truth.”

T’oma had said he would not believe without seeing the marks. Eight days later Yahusha came and offered him exactly what he had asked for. T’oma answered, “My Master and my Aluahim!” The berakah that follows is for everyone since: those who have not seen and have believed.

By a fire of coals Kĕpha had denied Him three times. By another fire, after breakfast, Yahusha asks him three times, “Do you love Me?” Each answer is met with work, not rebuke: “Feed My lambs … Shepherd My sheep … Feed My sheep.” He is restored by being trusted again.

The taught ones asked about times and seasons. Yahusha says those are in the Father's authority, and tells them what is theirs: power when the Ruach HaQadash comes, and a task that starts where they stand, in Yahrushalayim, and goes out to the end of the earth.

pool.theme: The promise is to you and to your children
pool.reflection: The crowd had been pierced to the heart by Kĕpha's words and asked what to do. He tells them: repent, be immersed in the Name of Yahusha Mashiach, and receive the gift of the Ruach HaQadash. The promise reaches them, their children, and “all who are far off.”

Kĕpha and Yahuchanon are on trial before the rulers for healing a lame man. Kĕpha quotes Tehillim 118 to the builders themselves: the stone you rejected has become the chief cornerstone. Deliverance is found in no one else.

pool.theme: He is not far from each one of us
pool.reflection: Sha’ul is speaking to philosophers in Athens who had a mizbe'ach inscribed to an unknown mighty one. He tells them the One who made every nation from one blood set their times and boundaries so that they would seek Him. He is near: “in Him we live and move and are.”

pool.theme: More baruk to give than to receive
pool.reflection: Sha’ul is saying farewell to the elders of Ephesos, who would not see his face again. He commits them to Aluahim and to the Word of His chen, which is able to build them up. He had worked with his own hands among them, and he leaves them a saying of the Master Yahusha about giving.

pool.theme: The power of Aluahim for deliverance
pool.reflection: Sha’ul is writing to Rome, the centre of the world's power, and says he is not ashamed of the Besorah. It is itself power, the power of Aluahim to deliver everyone who believes. He rests it on Ḥaḇaqquq: “the righteous shall live by belief.”

Being declared right by belief brings shalom with Aluahim and a standing in chen. Then Sha’ul says believers exult in pressures too, and traces why: pressure works endurance, endurance approvedness, approvedness expectation. That expectation does not disappoint, because His love has been poured into our hearts by the Ruach HaQadash.

Sha’ul reasons from what people will do. Hardly anyone dies for a righteous man; perhaps for a good one. Mashiach died for us when we were weak and still sinners. That is how Aluahim “proves His own love for us.” The proof was given before there was anything in us to love.

The chapter before ended with a cry, “Wretched man that I am!” This is the answer. For those in Mashiach Yahusha, who walk according to the Ruach, there is “now no condemnation.” The Torah of the Ruach of life has set them free from the law of sin and of death.

Those led by the Ruach of Aluahim are His sons. They were not given a ruach of bondage that leads back into fear. They were given the Ruach of adoption, and the proof is a cry: “Abba, Father.” Children are heirs, co-heirs with Mashiach, sharing His suffering and His esteem.

pool.theme: The Ruach helps in our weaknesses
pool.reflection: We do not know what we should pray, and Sha’ul counts himself in that “we.” The Ruach pleads for us with groanings that cannot be put into words, and He who searches hearts knows His mind. On that ground we know that all matters work together for good to those who love Aluahim.

Sha’ul asks what can be said to all this, and answers with a question nothing can meet. Then he argues from the greater gift to the lesser. He who did not spare His own Son has already given the most costly thing. He will not hold back the rest.

The list is Sha’ul's own life: pressure, distress, persecution, hunger, nakedness, danger, sword. He quotes Tehillim to show that the people of Aluahim have always known such things. None of them separates us from the love of Mashiach. “In all this,” in the midst of them, we overcome through Him who loved us.

Sha’ul ends the chapter with a list meant to leave nothing out: death and life, mal'akim and powers, the present and the future, height and depth, any other creature. None can separate us from the love of Aluahim “which is in Mashiach Yahusha our Master.”

pool.theme: With the heart and with the mouth
pool.reflection: The Word is near, in the mouth and in the heart; Sha’ul has just quoted Mosheh to say so. The heart believes that Aluahim raised Yahusha from the dead, and the mouth confesses Him as Master. Yashayahu is his witness: whoever trusts in Him “shall not be put to shame.”

For three chapters Sha’ul has worked through the hardest question he knew, Yasharal and the nations. He ends in praise. No one has been His counsellor, and no one has given to Him first. “Because of Him and through Him, and to Him, are all.”

“Therefore” reaches back over eleven chapters of the compassion of Aluahim. The fitting answer is our bodies, presented as a living offering, qadash and well-pleasing. The mind is to be renewed and not pressed into the shape of this world, so that we may prove what His good desire is.

Vengeance is taken out of our hands because it belongs to Another: “Vengeance is Mine, I shall repay,” says Yahuah. What is left to us is the proverb about a hungry enemy. Feed him and give him drink. Evil wins when it makes us like itself.

pool.theme: Love is completion of the Torah
pool.reflection: One debt is never paid off: to love one another. Sha’ul lists commands from the Ten Words, adultery, murder, theft, false witness, coveting, and says they are summed up in the word from Wayyiqra, “You shall love your neighbour as yourself.” Love does a neighbour no evil.

Sha’ul says what the Scriptures are for. They were written to teach us, so that through endurance and their encouragement we might have expectation. Then he prays that the Aluahim of endurance and encouragement would give one mind and one mouth to a qahal made of people who disagreed.

Sha’ul quotes Yashayahu's promise of the root of Yahshai, on whom the gentiles set their expectation. Then he prays for the believers in Rome: that Aluahim fill them with all joy and shalom in believing, and that they overflow with expectation “by the power of the Ruach HaQadash.”

Sha’ul has reminded the believers in Corinth that not many of them were wise, mighty or noble. What they have, they have in Mashiach Yahusha, who became for us wisdom from Aluahim, righteousness, set-apartness and redemption. So Yirmayahu's word holds: “He who boasts, let him boast in Yahuah.”

No eye has seen it, no ear heard it, no heart imagined it: what Aluahim has prepared for those who love Him. Sha’ul does not leave it wholly out of reach. “Aluahim has revealed them to us through His Ruach,” who searches even the depths of Aluahim.

Sha’ul wrote this to a qahal quarrelling over gifts. Every line is something love does or refuses to do: it does not envy, boast, or seek its own; it is not provoked; it keeps no account of evil. Put a name in place of “love” and it shows how far that person has come.

For now we see as in a mirror, dimly, and know in part. Sha’ul is content with that because of what is coming: “then face to face,” knowing as we have been known. Three things remain meanwhile, belief, expectation and love. “The greatest of these is love.”

pool.theme: Your labour is not in vain
pool.reflection: Sha’ul has spent the chapter on the resurrection, and he ends by taunting death with words from Hoshea. The overcoming is given through our Master Yahusha Mashiach. Because the dead are raised, he draws a conclusion about ordinary work: be steadfast, immovable, for it is not in vain.

pool.theme: Let all be done in love
pool.reflection: Five short commands close the letter. Four call for firmness: watch, stand fast in the belief, be men, be strong. The fifth governs how the other four are carried out: “Let all that you do be done in love.”

Sha’ul had been under pressure in Asia beyond his strength, despairing even of life. He begins the letter by blessing the Father of compassion, who comforts us in all our pressure. The comfort is meant to be passed on, to those who are in any pressure, out of what we ourselves received.

When Mosheh came down the mountain he veiled his face. Sha’ul says that in Mashiach the veil is taken away. “Where the Ruach of Yahuah is, there's freedom.” Seeing His esteem with unveiled face, we are changed into the same likeness, and it happens by degrees.

Sha’ul's outward man was wearing out, beaten and shipwrecked and hunted. He says the inward man is renewed day by day. He sets the present pressure, “slight” and “momentary,” on a scale against an everlasting weight of esteem. What is seen passes away. What is not seen is everlasting.

Anyone in Mashiach is a renewed creature. The old has passed away. All of it is from Aluahim, who restored us to chen with Himself and did not reckon our trespasses to us. Those who have been restored are then given the same word to carry to others.

Sha’ul is gathering a gift for the poor believers in Yahrushalayim. He will not have it given out of grief or under pressure. Each one decides in his own heart. And the giver is not left short: “Aluahim is able to make all chen overflow toward you,” enough for every good work.

pool.theme: My chen is sufficient for you
pool.reflection: Sha’ul asked three times for the thorn in his flesh to be taken away. The answer was no, and a promise with it: “My chen is sufficient for you, for My power is perfected in weakness.” So he stops hiding his weaknesses. They are where the power of Mashiach rests on him.

Sha’ul tells his own story in one sentence. He was impaled with Mashiach, and the life he now lives in the flesh he lives by belief in the Son of Aluahim, “who loved me and gave Himself for me.” He makes it personal. To set that aside would be to say Mashiach died for nothing.

The believers in Galatia had been called to freedom, and Sha’ul guards it from two sides. It is not a return to bondage, and it is not an opening for the flesh. Freedom is for serving one another through love, which is the Torah completed in one word.

Sha’ul has just listed the works of the flesh, in the plural. The fruit of the Ruach is one, and it has nine parts: love, joy, shalom, patience, kindness, goodness, trustworthiness, gentleness, self-control. It grows where the Ruach is. “Against such there is no Torah.”

When someone is overtaken in a trespass, those who walk by the Ruach are to set him straight, “in a ruach of meekness,” each one remembering that he could be tried too. Then the wider rule: bear one another's burdens. Sha’ul calls that completing the Torah of Mashiach.

pool.theme: In due season we shall reap
pool.reflection: Doing good is tiring, and Sha’ul knows it. He speaks as to farmers. There is a season between sowing and reaping, and the harvest comes “if we do not grow weary.” So do good to all as the occasion comes, and first to the household of the belief.

The chapter opens with what we were: dead in trespasses. Then, “But Aluahim.” Because of the great love with which He loved us, He made us alive together with Mashiach, raised us up, and seated us with Him. In the ages to come He means to show the riches of His chen in kindness toward us.

Deliverance is by chen, through belief, and that is not of ourselves: “it is the gift of Aluahim.” No one can boast of it. The works have their place afterwards. We were created in Mashiach Yahusha for good works which Aluahim prepared beforehand for us to walk in.

pool.theme: Exceedingly above what we ask or think
pool.reflection: Sha’ul has been praying on his knees that the believers would know the love of Mashiach. He ends by praising the One who can do more than he asked, more even than he thought to ask, “according to the power that is working in us.” To Him be esteem in the qahal to all generations.

Five things are to be put away: bitterness, wrath, displeasure, uproar and slander. Three take their place. Be kind, tenderhearted, forgiving one another. The measure and the motive are the same: “as Aluahim also forgave you in Mashiach.”

Children take after their father, and Sha’ul asks beloved children to imitate Aluahim. He says at once what that looks like. Walk in love, as Mashiach loved us and gave Himself for us, an offering to Aluahim “for a sweet smelling fragrance.”

Sha’ul writes this in chains. The strength is not our own: “in the Master and in the mightiness of His strength.” The armour is also His, the complete armour of Aluahim. With it there is power to stand against the schemes of the devil.

pool.theme: He who has begun a good work in you
pool.reflection: Sha’ul is a prisoner when he writes, and he prays for the believers at Philippi with joy. They had shared in the Besorah with him from the first day. He is persuaded of one thing about them. The work is Aluahim's, He began it, and He will carry it through until the day of Yahusha Mashiach.

pool.theme: That your love might extend more and more
pool.reflection: Sha’ul prays for love, and for love that grows “in knowledge and all discernment,” able to tell the things that differ. Love like that leads to a life sincere and without stumbling, filled with the fruit of righteousness that comes through Yahusha Mashiach.

The believers at Philippi are to go on obeying in Sha’ul's absence and to work out their deliverance with fear and trembling. The next line keeps that from becoming a burden. Aluahim is the one working in them, “both to desire and to work for His good pleasure.”

Sha’ul is near the end of his course and says he has not arrived. He has been laid hold of by Mashiach Yahusha, and he presses on to lay hold in return. He does one thing: forgetting what is behind, he reaches for what lies ahead, the prize of the high calling.

A man in chains writes “rejoice,” and then says it again. The joy is in Yahuah, which is why it can be “always.” Gentleness is to be shown to everyone. Both rest on four words at the end: “The Master is near.”

pool.theme: The shalom of Aluahim shall guard your hearts
pool.reflection: In place of worry Sha’ul puts prayer, in every matter, and it is to come with thanksgiving. He does not promise that every request is granted as asked. He promises a guard: the shalom of Aluahim, which is beyond understanding, set over hearts and minds through Mashiach Yahusha.

Sha’ul gives the mind something to dwell on: whatever is true, noble, righteous, clean, lovely, of good report. Then he moves from thinking to doing: what you learned and saw in me, “practise these.” The promise is the presence of the Aluahim of shalom.

pool.theme: I have learned to be content
pool.reflection: Sha’ul is thanking them for a gift and wants them to know he was not in want. Contentment was something he “learned,” in plenty and in hunger alike. The well-known line belongs to that lesson. He has strength for every condition through Mashiach who empowers him.

pool.theme: My Aluahim shall fill all your need
pool.reflection: The believers at Philippi had sent Sha’ul a gift out of what little they had. He cannot repay them. “My Aluahim” will, he says, and the measure is not their need but “His riches in esteem by Mashiach Yahusha.” The letter then turns to praise.

pool.theme: Rooted and built up in Him
pool.reflection: The way a person receives Mashiach Yahusha the Master is the way he goes on, by walking in Him. Sha’ul mixes a tree and a building: rooted, built up, established. The mark of a life settled like that is the last phrase, “overflowing in it with thanksgiving.”

Those raised with Mashiach are to seek and mind the matters above, where He is seated at the right hand of Aluahim. The reason is where their life now is. “You have died,” Sha’ul says, and your life is kept in the safest place there is, hidden with Mashiach in Aluahim.

Sha’ul speaks of character as clothing, put on by people who are already chosen, qadash and beloved. Compassion, kindness, humility, meekness, patience, and bearing with one another: forgive as Mashiach forgave you. Over all of these goes love. The shalom of Aluahim is to rule in the heart, “and be filled with thanks.”

pool.theme: Let the Word of Mashiach dwell in you richly
pool.reflection: The Word is to live in the qahal as in a home, richly. It comes out in teaching one another and in singing psalms and songs of praise. Then Sha’ul gathers up everything else, every word and deed, to be done “in the Name of the Master Yahusha,” with thanks.

pool.theme: As to the Master and not to men
pool.reflection: Sha’ul first wrote this to servants, people whose work was not their own and who were seldom thanked for it. Whatever the task, do it from the heart. The reward comes from the Master: “It is the Master, Mashiach, you serve.”

Three commands are given, with “always,” “without ceasing” and “in all circumstances” attached. Sha’ul does not say to give thanks for all circumstances. He says in them. People often ask what Aluahim's desire is for them, and here it is stated plainly.

pool.theme: He who calls you is trustworthy
pool.reflection: Sha’ul prays that the Aluahim of shalom would set them completely apart and keep ruach, being and body blameless at the coming of the Master. That is a great deal to ask. The next verse says why he can ask it. The One who calls is trustworthy, “who also shall do it.”

The believers there had been shaken by reports that the day of Yahuah had already come. Sha’ul prays to the One who “has loved us and given us everlasting encouragement and good expectation, through chen,” asking that He encourage their hearts and establish them in every good word and work.

Sha’ul has just said that not all have belief. “But the Master is trustworthy.” He will establish and guard them from the wicked one. Then a prayer for their hearts, that they be directed “into the love of Aluahim and into the endurance for Mashiach.”

pool.theme: Mashiach Yahusha came to save sinners
pool.reflection: Sha’ul had persecuted the qahal, and he never forgot it. He calls himself the foremost of sinners, and says that is why he received compassion: to show how patient Yahusha Mashiach is with those who will believe after him. The thought turns him to praise of the Sovereign of the ages.

Some thought reverence was a way to get rich. Sha’ul says there is great gain in it when it comes with contentment. We brought nothing into the world and can carry nothing out. With food and covering, he says, “we shall be satisfied.”

pool.theme: The living Aluahim, who gives us richly
pool.reflection: This is a charge for those who are rich in the present age. They are not to be high-minded or to trust in riches, which are uncertain. Aluahim gives richly “for enjoyment.” The rich are to do good and be ready to share, and so take hold of everlasting life.

This is Sha’ul's last letter, written from prison to a younger man inclined to be timid. The gift of Aluahim in Timothy is like a fire that needs stirring. What Aluahim gives is not a ruach of cowardice, “but of power and of love and of self-control.”

This may have been a saying the early believers recited together. To die with Him is to live with Him, and to endure is to reign with Him. The warning about denying Him stands. The last line goes beyond our failures: “If we are not trustworthy, He remains trustworthy.” He cannot deny Himself.

pool.theme: All Scripture is breathed by Aluahim
pool.reflection: When Sha’ul wrote this, the Scripture Timothy had known from childhood was the Torah, the Naḇi'im and the Writings. All of it is breathed by Aluahim and useful: for teaching, reproof, setting straight and instruction in righteousness. It equips the man of Aluahim “for every good work.”

Sha’ul knows his death is near. He looks back in three short clauses: the good fight fought, the race finished, the belief guarded. Then he looks ahead to the crown of righteousness. It is not for him only. It is for “all those loving His appearing.”

pool.theme: The saving Gift of Aluahim has appeared
pool.reflection: The chen that saves also teaches. It instructs us to renounce wickedness and to live sensibly, righteously and reverently now, while we look for the appearing of our Saviour Yahusha Mashiach. He gave Himself to redeem us from all lawlessness and to cleanse a people for Himself, “ardent for good works.”

Sha’ul has just described what we once were: foolish, disobedient, led astray. “But when the kindness and the love of Aluahim our Saviour toward man appeared, He saved us.” Works of righteousness we had done played no part. It was His compassion, with a washing of rebirth and renewal by the Ruach HaQadash.

pool.theme: The Word of Aluahim is living and working
pool.reflection: The Word is living, at work, and sharper than a two-edged sword. It reaches where nothing else does and judges “the thoughts and intentions of the heart.” No creature is hidden from Him. The verses that follow tell where someone so laid bare may go: to the throne of chen.

Our Kohen gadol has passed through the shamayim, and He knows what weakness is. He was “tried in all respects as we are, apart from sin.” So we are told to come boldly. The throne we come to is one of chen, where compassion is received and help comes at the right time.

Hold fast the confession of our expectation without yielding. The reason has nothing to do with our grip: “He who promised is trustworthy.” Then, be concerned for one another and stir up love and good works. The writer names the plain way to do that, which is not to give up assembling together.

pool.theme: The proof of what is not seen
pool.reflection: Before the long roll of those who lived by belief, the writer says what belief is: the substance of what is expected and the proof of what is not seen. By it we understand that the ages were prepared by the Word of Aluahim. What is seen came from what is not visible.

The “cloud of witnesses” are those of the chapter before, Noaḥ, Aḇraham, Mosheh and the rest, who finished their course. We lay aside whatever weighs us down and run ours. Our eyes are to be on Yahusha, who endured the stake for the joy set before Him and has sat down.

pool.theme: Afterward it yields the peaceable fruit
pool.reflection: The writer does not pretend discipline is pleasant. At the time it is grievous. The word to hold is “afterward”: it yields the peaceable fruit of righteousness to those trained by it. So he takes up Yashayahu's words about strengthening drooping hands and weak knees, and making straight paths.

Contentment is commanded here, and a reason is given that money cannot supply. He Himself has said, “I shall never leave you nor forsake you,” the promise made to Yahusha son of Nun. So we can answer with a line from Tehillim: “Yahuah is my helper, I shall not fear.”

pool.theme: The same yesterday and today and forever
pool.reflection: Remember those who spoke the Word of Aluahim to you, the writer says. Consider how their lives turned out, and imitate their belief. Leaders come and go. The One they trusted does not: “Yahusha Mashiach is the same yesterday and today and forever.”

There are offerings still to bring, and they are brought through Him. One is praise, “the fruit of our lips, giving thanks to His Name.” The other is doing good and sharing. With such offerings, the writer says, Aluahim is well pleased.

pool.theme: That great Shepherd of the sheep
pool.reflection: This berakah closes the letter. The Aluahim of shalom brought up our Master Yahusha from the dead, the great Shepherd of the sheep, through the blood of the everlasting berith. The prayer is that He would equip us for every good work and Himself work in us what pleases Him.

pool.theme: Let endurance have a perfect work
pool.reflection: Ya'aqoḇ writes to the twelve tribes in the dispersion. He calls trials a cause for joy because of what they do: the proving of belief works endurance, and endurance makes a person complete. When we cannot see how, we are to ask Aluahim for wisdom. He “gives to all generously and without reproach.”

Just before this, Ya'aqoḇ has said that no one is enticed to evil by Aluahim. What comes down from Him is every good and perfect gift. Sun and moon change and cast moving shadows. The Father who made them has “no change, nor shadow of turning.” He brought us forth by the Word of truth.

pool.theme: Swift to hear, slow to speak
pool.reflection: Three speeds are given: swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath. Most of us have them in the opposite order. Ya'aqoḇ gives a reason that removes the usual excuse for anger: “the wrath of man does not work the righteousness of Aluahim.”

A man looks in a mirror, walks away, and forgets what he saw. Ya'aqoḇ says that is what hearing without doing amounts to. The other man looks into “the perfect Torah, that of freedom,” and continues in it. He is the one who is baruk, and he is baruk in the doing.

Ya'aqoḇ has described a wisdom that is earthly and full of envy and self-seeking. The wisdom from above can be recognised by how it behaves: clean first, then peaceable, gentle, ready to obey, full of compassion and good fruits. Those who make shalom sow in shalom and reap righteousness.

“Aluahim resists the proud, but gives chen to the humble,” a line from Mishle. So Ya'aqoḇ says to be subject to Aluahim and to resist the devil, who will flee. The promise in the middle is for anyone who takes the step: “Draw near to Aluahim and He shall draw near to you.”

pool.theme: Until the early and latter rain
pool.reflection: The farmer has done his work. He cannot make the rain come, so he waits for it, because the fruit of the earth is precious to him. Ya'aqoḇ tells the brothers to be patient in the same way and to establish their hearts: “the coming of the Master has drawn near.”

pool.theme: You have heard of the endurance of Iyoḇ
pool.reflection: For an example of suffering and patience Ya'aqoḇ points to the naḇi'im who spoke in the Name of Yahuah, and to Iyoḇ. We count those who endure as baruk. And we have seen how it ended for Iyoḇ, which shows what Yahuah is like: “very sympathetic and compassionate.”

There is an instruction for each condition. Whoever is suffering should pray, whoever is glad should sing psalms, and whoever is sick should call for the elders of the qahal. Believers are to confess to one another and pray for one another. “The earnest prayer of a righteous one accomplishes much.”

pool.theme: The living Word of Aluahim, which remains forever
pool.reflection: Kĕpha tells believers scattered through Asia to love one another fervently, and bases it on how they were born again: of incorruptible seed, through the living Word of Aluahim. He quotes Yashayahu. Grass withers and the flower falls, “but the Word of Aluahim remains forever.”

pool.theme: Out of darkness into His marvellous light
pool.reflection: Kĕpha gives believers from the nations the titles spoken over Yasharal at Sinai: a chosen race, a royal kehunnah, a qadash nation, a people for a possession. Then words from Hoshea. They were once not a people and are now the people of Aluahim, called so that they would proclaim His praises.

Kĕpha sums up life together in five words: like-minded, sympathetic, loving as brothers, tenderhearted, humble-minded. Then the harder part, which is to give berakah in return for evil and reviling. The reason is their calling. They are to inherit a berakah, so they hand one on.

pool.theme: Love covers a great number of sins
pool.reflection: “Above all,” Kĕpha says, have fervent love, and he quotes Mishle on what love does with offences. Then two plain applications. Welcome one another without grumbling. And use whatever gift you have received to serve, “as good trustees of the manifold chen of Aluahim.”

Kĕpha writes to believers under pressure. Humble yourselves under the mighty hand of Aluahim, and He will lift you up in due time. Part of that humbling is to stop carrying what was never ours to carry: “casting all your worry upon Him, for He is concerned about you.”

pool.theme: After you have suffered a while
pool.reflection: Kĕpha does not hide the suffering, and he sets a limit on it: “a while.” Against it he sets an everlasting esteem. The Aluahim of all chen, who called them, will Himself perfect, establish, strengthen and settle them. Four verbs, and Aluahim is the subject of each.

Kĕpha names a chain of seven things to be added to belief with all diligence: uprightness, knowledge, self-control, endurance, reverence, brotherly affection, love. Belief is the beginning and love is the end. Where these are present and increasing, a person is neither idle nor fruitless.

Mockers were asking where the promise of His coming was. Kĕpha answers that with Yahuah one day is as a thousand years. What looks like slowness is patience. He is “not wishing that any should perish but that all should come to repentance.”

This is the message Yahuchanon heard from Yahusha Himself: Aluahim is light, and in Him is no darkness at all. To claim fellowship with Him and walk in darkness is a lie. To walk in the light brings fellowship with one another, and cleansing from all sin by the blood of His Son.

pool.theme: He is trustworthy and righteous to forgive
pool.reflection: Two “if we say” lines come before this, and one “if we confess.” To claim we have no sin is to mislead ourselves. To confess it is to meet Him as He is: “trustworthy and righteous to forgive us the sins and cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”

pool.theme: We have an Intercessor with the Father
pool.reflection: Yahuchanon writes as an old man to his “little children.” He writes so that they do not sin. He also knows them, so he adds what is true when they do. There is an Intercessor with the Father, Yahusha Mashiach, a righteous One, the atoning offering for our sins and for all the world.

“See what love,” Yahuchanon says, as if pointing at something. We are called children of Aluahim, and it is true now. What we shall be has not yet been revealed. He is sure of this much: when He is revealed, “we shall be like Him, for we shall see Him as He is.”

Love is known by what Yahusha did: He laid down His life for us. Yahuchanon brings it home at once. A brother is in need, and I have this world's goods. The test of love is whether I open my hand. “Let us not love in word or in tongue, but in deed and in truth.”

Love is of Aluahim, and Yahuchanon says where to look to learn what it is. We did not love Him first. “He loved us and sent His Son to be an atoning offering for our sins.” No one has seen Aluahim. When we love one another He stays in us, and His love is perfected.

Yahuchanon has been speaking of boldness in the day of judgment. Fear expects punishment, and perfect love drives that fear out. This love does not start with us. “We love Him because He first loved us.”

Love for Aluahim is shown in guarding His commands, and Yahuchanon, who knew Yahusha's yoke at first hand, says they “are not heavy.” Whoever is born of Aluahim overcomes the world. The overcoming is our belief that Yahusha is the Son of Aluahim.

Yahuchanon wrote so that those who believe in the Name of the Son of Aluahim may know, and not merely hope, that they have everlasting life. The life is in His Son. Knowing that gives boldness in prayer: whatever we ask according to His desire, “He hears us.”

The elder writes to his friend Gaios and prays that he may do well and be in health, as his inner life already is. Brothers had come and told how Gaios walks in the truth. The old man had no greater joy than to hear such news of his children.

pool.theme: Keep yourselves in the love of Aluahim
pool.reflection: Yahuḏah has warned at length about those who creep in and corrupt. Then he turns: “But you, beloved ones.” He gives four things to do: build yourselves up on your most qadash belief, pray in the Ruach HaQadash, keep yourselves in the love of Aluahim, and look for the compassion of our Master Yahusha Mashiach.

pool.theme: Him who is able to keep you from stumbling
pool.reflection: He has just told them to keep themselves in the love of Aluahim. He ends with the One who is able to keep them, and to present them blameless before His esteem “with exceeding joy.” To the only wise Aluahim our Saviour belong esteem, greatness, might and authority.

pool.theme: I am the First and the Last
pool.reflection: Yahuchanon is an exile on the island of Patmos, and when he sees the risen Yahusha he falls at His feet as dead. A right hand is laid on him, and he hears the words spoken so often in Scripture: “Do not be afraid.” The living One was dead and is alive forever, and holds the keys of the grave and of death.

pool.theme: I stand at the door and knock
pool.reflection: This is said to the qahal at Laodikeia, lukewarm and sure it needed nothing. His reproof is itself a sign of love: “As many as I love, I reprove and discipline.” He is outside, knocking. Anyone who hears and opens will have Him come in and share a meal.

These are the ones who have come out of the great distress. They serve before the throne, and He who sits on it spreads His Tent over them. Hunger, thirst and scorching heat are over. The Lamb is their shepherd and leads them to fountains of waters of life, “and Aluahim shall wipe away every tear.”

The promise made in Wayyiqra is heard again at the end, from the throne: Aluahim will dwell with men, they shall be His people, and He Himself shall be with them. He wipes away every tear. Death, mourning, crying and pain belong to the former matters. “Write, for these words are true and trustworthy.”

Yahusha speaks near the close of the book. He is coming, and His reward is with Him. He is the Aleph and the Taw, the Beginning and the End. Those who do His commands are called baruk. The tree of life, guarded since Ĕḏen, is theirs, and the gates of the city are open to them.

Yahusha names Himself the Root and the Offspring of Dawiḏ, the bright and Morning Star. Then the invitation goes out from every side, the Ruach, the bride, and each one who hears. It is for anyone thirsty: “take the water of life without paying!” Yashayahu gave the same call.

pool.theme: Take off the garment of your sorrow
pool.reflection: Baruḵ speaks to Yahrushalayim as to a mourner. She is to take off the garment of sorrow and affliction and put on the beauty of the esteem that comes from Aluahim, with a robe of righteousness and a diadem. The clothes are a gift. She has only to put them on.

Ben Sira begins his book with a question nobody can answer: who can count the sand, the drops of rain, the days of eternity? Wisdom is like that, older than all things and beyond searching out. One alone is wise, “sitting upon his throne.”

pool.theme: The fear of Yahuah delights the heart
pool.reflection: Ben Sira does not treat the fear of Yahuah as a gloomy thing. It delights the heart, he says, and gives gladness, joy and long life. He looks to the end as well. For the one who fears Yahuah, “it will go well at the end.”

The one who fears Yahuah is not timid, Ben Sira says, because of whom he looks to. The eyes of Yahuah are on those who love Him. He is a shelter from the hot wind, shade at noon, and a guard against stumbling. “He lifts up the nephesh and gives light to the eyes.”

Ben Sira has just described the kohen gadol Shim‛on coming out of the House in his splendour, and he turns to the people with a berakah. Bless the Aluahim of all, who does great things and deals with us according to His chesed. He asks for gladness of heart and shalom in Yasharal.

This is from the Wisdom of Shelomoh, on the death of the righteous. To the foolish they seemed simply to have died, and their going was called a disaster. The writer says where they are: “in the hand of Aluahim.” They are at shalom.

The writer reasons from creation to compassion. Aluahim loves all things that exist, since He would not have made what He hated, and nothing could last unless He willed it. So He overlooks men's sins “that they may repent,” and spares all things because they are His.

pool.theme: Do not turn your face away
pool.reflection: Tobit believes he is about to die and is instructing his son Tobias. Give from what you have, he says, and do not begrudge it. Do not turn your face from any poor man. If you have little, “do not be afraid to give according to the little you have.”
